translations.text: Here begins the first book of Boethius. The complaint of Boethius. On the instability of Fortune.
I who once composed songs with flourishing zeal,
alas, weeping, am forced to take up sorrowful measures. I, who once made joyful songs, must now make songs of lament out of necessity.
Behold, the torn Muses dictate to me what I must write. Look now, the grieving Muses

teach me to write. What grieves me grieves them. Those who once taught me joyful songs now teach me songs of weeping. And elegies, that is, wretched ones, wet my face with true tears, that is, tears that are not feigned. And they fill my eyes with earnest tears.
These companions, at least, no terror could overcome
so that they would not follow my path. No one could deter these companions from going along with me. As if he were saying: Though I am robbed of other things, no one could rob me of my learning.
Once the glory of my happy and flourishing youth,
they now console the fate of a sad old man. Once they were the glory of my youth; now they console me, an old man, in my misfortune.
For unexpected old age has come, hastened by evils.

There is need of this as well, because hasty old age has come upon me unexpectedly, hurried on by hardships. And grief has ordered its own age to be in me, that is, "its own" because it forces one to grow old sooner. And grief has made me old.
Untimely grey hairs pour down from my head. Because of these things I grow grey before my time.
And loose skin trembles on my exhausted body. And slack skin quivers on a body without strength. That is to say, my limbs tremble beneath slack skin.
Happy is the death of men that does not thrust itself into the sweet years
and that comes to the sorrowful when it is often called. Blessed is the death that does not come in pleasant times and does not delay when it is wished for in sorrow. Alas,
with how deaf an ear it turns away from the wretched. Ah, all too much! How poorly it hears the wretched. And, cruel,
it refuses to close weeping eyes. And how unwillingly it, cruel as it is, closes their weeping eyes.
While faithless fortune favoured me with fleeting goods. As long as fortune attended me in all my wealth, which was unstable, as it now appears.
the sad hour had almost overwhelmed my head. At that time the sorrowful hour had nearly taken me, I mean the last hour.
Now, because, clouded over, she has changed her deceitful face,
my impious life drags out unwelcome delays. Because she has now forsaken me, my toilsome life now lengthens my term.
Why, friends, did you so often boast that I was happy? Why did you always call me happy, my friends? Where is that happiness now?
He who has fallen did not stand on a steady footing.
He who fell never truly stood firm! If he had stood firm, he would not have fallen. An argument from incompatible things, for standing and falling are incompatible.

ON THE ENTRANCE OF PHILOSOPHY, AND HER APPEARANCE. While I was silently pondering these things by myself, while I considered this silently in my mind, and was recording my tearful complaint by means of the pen, and I wrote such a lamentable complaint with the stylus, a woman seemed to stand over my head. Lo, I saw a woman standing above me, of a countenance deserving great reverence, of very venerable appearance.
With burning eyes. With earnest eyes. And piercing, beyond the common power of men.

And seeing more penetratingly than any human can see. For philosophy sees even the deep things of God. With vivid colour. With youthful colour. She does not grow old. And of inexhaustible vigour. And of great strength, and unfailing! For she reaches from end to end mightily. Although she was so full of age. Though she was so old. That in no way would she be believed to belong to our age. That no one would believe her to be of the same age as himself. For she always was. Of a stature whose measure was uncertain. Of doubtful size in her growth. I could not tell how big she was.
For now indeed she restrained herself to the common measure of men.

For at one time she drew herself down here to our measure, because she sometimes considers human things. But now she seemed to strike the heaven with the top of her highest crown. At another time she seemed to me to touch the heaven with her uppermost head, because she knows astronomy. And when she had raised her head higher, she penetrated even heaven itself. When she lifted her head high up, it passed beyond the heaven; she does that by searching out divine things. And she baffled the gaze of those looking at her. And so she deceived the eyes of those who gazed at her.
CONCERNING HER GARMENT. Her garments were made of the finest threads, with subtle craftsmanship, of indissoluble material. Her garment was fine and beautiful,

and of firm material. That garment is precious in which these three things are present. Her garment, that is the liberal arts. That it is fine, the arguments make it so; that it is beautiful, the figures of thought and of speech (dianoeos and lexeos) make it so. That they are firm, the truth makes it so. When a true conclusion follows from true premises, no one can do anything against it. Therefore there is always firmness in truth. Which she herself had woven with her own hands, as I afterwards learned from her own disclosure. That garment she made herself, as I afterwards learned from her. Whence could the arts have come, except from the wisdom of God? Their appearance a certain darkness of neglected age had covered, as it is wont to cover smoky images. Their images were dulled by age,

like smoke-blackened paintings. Or thus: old neglect had darkened their beauty. For when no one practises the arts, they are forgotten. On the lowest border of these was read, woven in, a Greek π. At the very bottom of the garment was written the Greek P. That signifies the practical life, that is, the active life. But in the upper part was read θ. At the very top stood theta. That signifies the theoretical life, that is, the contemplative life. And between the two letters there appeared to be marked certain steps in the manner of ladders.

And between the letters there stood, drawn as it were, ladder-rungs, or the steps of a stair. By which there was an ascent from the lower letter to the higher. By which one could climb from the lower letter to the upper one. For the saints and the wise proceed from the active life to the contemplative. Yet the hands of certain violent men had torn that same garment. Certain robbers had torn that same garment. And they had carried off such pieces as each one could. And they had gone off with their pieces, whatever each one could snatch away. For the Epicureans and the Stoics and the Academics quarrelled, and divided themselves into various sects.
And her right hand indeed held books, but her left a sceptre.
In her right hand she carried books, in which were the liberal arts; in her left a sceptre, because she is a queen. She said: "By me kings reign, and my throne is in a pillar of cloud."

ON THE EXPULSION OF THE FLATTERING MUSES. When she saw the poetic Muses standing by our bed. When she saw the verse-makers standing before my bed. And dictating words to my weeping. And reciting tears to me with their words. Stirred a little. At once somewhat angered by this. And inflamed, with fierce eyes. And looking threateningly.
She said. She asked: "Who has allowed these stage harlots, that is, theatre harlots, to come near this sick man?"

Who let these whores, used to the theatre, in here to this sick man? Harlots used to be prostituted in the vaults (fornices) of the theatre; that is where the word fornication comes from. Just as those women corrupted men with their enticements, so these also did with their wretched words. That is why he calls them harlots. Or, by "stage harlots" he means the stage Muses, such as comedies and tragedies were, which also harmed people, because comedies offered a man laughter and tragedies grief. Who not only would not soothe his pains with any remedies, but would even feed them with sweet poisons. They do not heal his pain at all, but even increase it with the sweet poison of their words. For these are the ones who kill the rich crop of the fruits of reason with the barren thorns of the passions. These are the ones who choke the harvest and the sown field of reason

with the thorns of desire. That is, with their flattering talk they make a man forget his reason. And they accustom men's minds to the disease; they do not free them. And they push men's minds into the sickness; they do not release them. But if your blandishments had drawn away some profane man, as you commonly do, I would think it less troublesome to bear. But if you had led astray from me some outsider with your caresses, as you often do, that would not weigh on me so much. For our labours would suffer no harm in him. In him I would lose nothing of my labours.
But this man, raised on Eleatic studies,

and Academic [studies], I do not allow to be taken from me. But this man, schooled in Greek learning and thoroughly taught in the Academy. But go away instead, you Sirens, sweet even to destruction. Get away, you Sirens, delightful all the way to ruin. Sirens are sea-creatures; their song puts sailors to sleep, and they suffer shipwreck. And leave him to my Muses, to be cared for and healed. And leave me to nourish his mind and heal it with my songs.

Rebuked by these words, that chorus cast its face down to the ground more sorrowfully. Then that company, thus rebuked, sank down. And confessing its shame with a blush, it sadly went out over the threshold. And reddening with shame, it left. But I, whose sight had grown dim, sunk in tears,
and unable to make out who this woman of such commanding authority might be, was astounded. But I was then amazed as to who the woman was who carried herself so powerfully.

I could not recognize her, because my eye was dimmed, full of tears. And with my gaze fixed on the ground. And I, looking down in front of me. I silently began to watch what she would do next. I began, keeping silent, to watch

what she would do after that. Then she came closer and sat down at the far end of my couch. Then, coming nearer at once, she sat at the very end of my bed. And looking at my face, heavy with grief. And looking at my countenance, heavy from weeping. And cast down to the ground by sorrow. And bowed down by sadness. With these verses she lamented the disturbance of our mind. She lamented my dejection with these verses.
THE LAMENT OF PHILOSOPHY OVER THE SICK MAN. Alas, how dulled the mind is, sunk in the steep depth. Ah, how very badly a man's mind fares when it is suddenly plunged into the pit.
And having abandoned its own light, that is, natural wisdom,

it strives to go into outer darkness, that is, into folly, which is against its nature. And how eagerly it then hurries out of the light into the darkness. How it deprives itself of its comfort and attaches itself to despair. When does it do so? Whenever harmful care,
swollen by earthly winds,
grows beyond measure.
When his cares, because of his former prosperity, become immoderate. For if he was rich before, then when he suddenly lacks it, it weighs on him. This man, once free,
accustomed to go under the open sky into the heavenly paths,
beheld the lights of the rosy sun,

looked upon the stars of the cold moon. This man was accustomed to think about the heavenly courses while he was [?] at ease, and in clear weather he observed the courses of the sun and of the moon. And as victor he held, grasped by numbers,
whatever star runs its wandering courses,
turned through various orbits.

And he also knew by number the courses that any planet takes, crossing into the courses of the other planets. He knew well the count of months and the count of years of each of their courses. For he knew that Saturn goes around the heaven in thirty years, Jupiter in twelve, Mars in two, the sun in one year, Mercury and Venus within a year, the moon in thirty days; and that each of them runs counter to another. As the moon does to the sun, when an eclipse of the sun occurs; and as we saw Mars run against the moon when it was three nights old, and pass across the middle of it, not from below but from above. Therefore he says: "turned through various orbits."
Moreover, accustomed to search out the causes
whence the roaring blasts stir up the waters of the sea.

He wanted also to know what drives the winds that stir up the sea. Virgil thought that Aeolus let them out. He lets them out who brings forth the winds out of his treasuries. What spirit turns the stable sphere – that is, stable because it turns and does not fall. Who drives the unwearying heaven around? Who but the Spirit of God?
Or why the star that is to sink into the western waves
rises from the ruddy east. Or how the signs that go westward to their setting come back to the east. The heaven in which they stand drives them around.
What tempers the gentle hours of spring. What makes the spring so mild.
So that it adorns the earth with rosy flowers. So that it adorns the earth with flowers. This is done by the sun turning back hither from the winter circle.
Who granted that fruitful autumn, with heavy
that is, ripe, grapes, should flow, that is, abound, in a full year? And who granted that autumn should come laden with ripe berries
in a plentiful year? And – that is, he was accustomed –
to give the various causes of hidden nature. And he could give answers about many hidden things, what this and that means.
Now he lies with the light of his mind exhausted. All this he knew; now he is witless; now he has been deprived of the strength of his mind.
And his neck weighed down with heavy chains. And chained about the neck, that is, held fast by despair.
And bearing a face bowed down by the weight. And bent down by that burden.
He is forced, alas, to gaze upon the dull earth. He looks against his will at the earth; he thinks, alas, upon the senseless earth, which makes people senseless.
THE PHYSICIAN'S TEST: WHETHER THE SICK MAN'S ILLNESS IS DEADLY. "But it is time," she said, "for medicine rather than for complaint."

Now, however, it is more the time for healing than for lamenting. Then indeed, fixing all her gaze on me, she said – and, looking closely at me after that, she asked: "Are you he who, once nourished with our milk,
brought up on our food, had grown into the strength of a manly [?] mind?

Were you not suckled with my milk and brought up on my nourishment [?] until you rose to a man's understanding? Are you not he? And yet – truly – we had given you such arms. I also gave you such armour, which would have protected you with unconquered firmness, under which you would have been kept safe, unless you had first thrown them away – if you had not willingly thrown them away. Do you recognize me? Do you know me?
Why are you silent? Why are you silent? Have you fallen silent from shame or from bewilderment? Whether from shame

or from fright? I would rather it were from shame, that is, because reverence produces shame, while a guilty conscience produces stupor. I would prefer it to be from shame, that is, from good breeding, and from modesty, and from restraint, and from respectfulness. But, as I see, stupor has overwhelmed you, that is, your conscience torments you. But it seems to me that fear is hurting you; you know yourself to be guilty. And when she saw that I was not only silent but entirely tongueless and mute. When she then saw me not merely silent but as if mute and tongueless. She gently laid her hand on my breast. Then she laid her hand softly on my breast.
"And there is no danger," she said. "No danger," she said. "He is suffering from lethargy. He has caught forgetfulness, the common disease of deluded minds.

the common sickness of those who are out of their wits. He has forgotten himself for a little while. He has forgotten himself a little. He will easily remember, if indeed he first recognizes us. He will remember himself well,

provided he first recognizes me. And so that he may be able to do so, and so that he can recognize me, let us wipe his eyes for a little, darkened by the cloud of mortal things. So let us wipe his eyes, which are clouded by the mist of mortal things." Thus she spoke. Thus she said. And gathering her garment into a fold, she dried my eyes, which were streaming with tears. And with the gathered cloth of her garment she wiped my weeping eyes.
ON HIS ILLUMINATION. Then, the night having been dispelled, the darkness left me. At once, with the night driven away, the darkness left me.
And my former strength returned to my eyes.
And the light of my eyes came back to me, such as I had had before. As it happens when the stars are massed together by the headlong wind, when the stars are covered over by a cloud-making wind.
and the sky stands heavy with cloudy rains, and the sky is altogether ready for thick rains,
the sun hides, and the sun does not shine,
and night is poured down from above upon the earth,

while the stars have not yet come into the sky; and it becomes night before the stars shine in the sky. If Boreas, sent forth from the Thracian cave, that is, from the valleys of Thrace, should strike it. As happens when afterwards the north wind blowing from Thrace scatters that night,
and unlocks the shut-in day,
and makes bright the day that was dark before, Phoebus flashes forth. And then the sun shines. And, quivering with sudden light,
he strikes the wondering eyes with his rays.

And the sun, suddenly shining, darts into the eyes of the people who are marvelling. In just the same way, when the mists were dissolved, I drank in the sky. Just so, when the mist was scattered, I saw the sky. And I recovered my mind so as to recognize the face of the one who was healing me. And I came to my senses enough to recognize her, and that she was the physician. And so, when I turned my eyes upon her
When I let my eyes rest on her and fixed my gaze, and looked at her closely, I recognized my nurse, Philosophy.

I recognized her to be my nurse, in whose house I had lived from my youth. In whose dwelling I lived from childhood. And I said: "O mistress of all virtues, why have you come down from the pole of heaven into this solitude of our exile?" And so, said I, what did you want, mistress of all virtues, coming from heaven here into this wilderness of my exile? "Or is it so that you too, accused along with me, may be harried by false charges?" Or rather, is it so that you too, accused, may be troubled by false charges and brought into distress?
"Should I desert you, my pupil?" she said.

"Should I then abandon you," she said, "my home-reared one? And should I not share with you, in common labor, the burden that you have taken up because of hatred for my name?" And should I not take an equal share in your hardships, which you suffer because of hatred for me? "But indeed, it was not right for Philosophy to leave the path of the innocent unaccompanied." Truly, it never befitted Philosophy to let the innocent go on without her.
"Should I, then, fear accusation against myself?" Should I, you say, fear accusation against me? "And shudder at it as if it were something new?" And be frightened of it, as of some new thing?

BETTER THINGS ARE NOT TO BE HOPED FOR IN NEW TIMES THAN IN OLD. "For do you think that wisdom has now for the first time been assailed by dangers among wicked ways?" Do you think that wisdom has only now been driven into distress by the wicked?

"Did we not often, among the ancients too, before the age of our Plato, fight a great battle against the rashness of folly?" Did I not often, even among the ancients before Plato's time, fight a hard battle

against the boldness of fools? "And while Plato was still alive, did not his teacher Socrates, with me standing by, win the victory of an unjust death?" And while Plato was living, did not his master Socrates triumph over death, with me looking on? "Afterwards the Epicurean mob and the Stoic, and the others, each for his own part, strove to go and seize his inheritance," And then the Epicureans and Stoics, and others too, hurried to snatch his inheritance, each for his own share, "and dragged me off as if I were part of the plunder, though I protested and resisted." And they pulled at me, as people do when dividing plunder, while I cried out against it and resisted.
"They tore the robe that I had woven with my own hands." They tore my garment, which I had made myself.
"And having torn little shreds off it," And with patches torn off it, "believing that I had yielded to them wholly, they went away."
Thinking they had all of me, they went off with it. "In these, since some traces of our dress seemed to appear,

For some semblance of my garb [?] was on those plunderers. Rata imprudentia meos esse familiares: Their folly, believing they were my intimates. Folly, supposing that they were my close companions, peruertit nonnullos eorum errore profanae multitudinis: led some of them astray by the error of the profane multitude. It deceived some of them with the false belief that always goes about among the accursed multitude. They took the multitude's word that they were wise. Quodsi nec fugam Anaxagorae nouisti: But if you have not known of the flight of Anaxagoras. If you have never heard how the Stoic philosopher Anaxagoras fled, that is, so that he would not suffer torture, and was therefore long in exile; nec Socratis uenenum: nor the poison of Socrates. Nor how Socrates was forced to drink hemlock because he said that Jupiter and Apollo were dead. He also said that an oath sworn by the living dog was worth more than one sworn by dead Jupiter. Nec Zenonis tormenta: Nor the tortures of Zeno.

Nor what torments the philosopher Zeno suffered. He bit off his own tongue because he would not betray the men he knew to be conspirators. Quoniam sunt peregrina: Because these things are foreign. If you do not know about it because it happened in a foreign land, I mean in Greece, at scire potuisti Canios: yet you could have known men like Canius. But you could know men like Canius, who lived under the emperor Gaius. At Senecas: And men like Seneca. And men like Seneca, who was killed at Nero's command. At Soranos: And men like Soranus. And also Soranus. Quorum memoria nec uetusta nec incelebris est: Whose memory is neither old nor obscure. The memory of them is not yet old, nor is it without fame. Quos nihil aliud detraxit in mortem: Whom nothing else dragged to death. Nothing else brought them to their death,
Nisi quod uidebantur instituti nostris moribus: Except that they seemed to have been trained in our ways.
Except that they had been taught according to my custom. Dissimillimi studiis improborum: Most unlike the wicked in their pursuits. Unlike the zeal of the harmful.

ADVERSITY IS NOT TO BE FEARED. Itaque nihil est quod ammireris si agitamur in hoc salo uitae circumflantibus procellis: So there is nothing for you to wonder at if we are tossed about on this sea of life by storms blowing all around us. You need not wonder at all if we are tossed about in this sea by winds driving at us from every side. That is, if we suffer hardships in this perilous life at the hands of many persecutors. Quibus hoc maxime propositum est displicere pessimis: For our chief aim is to displease the worst of men. For we want to displease the wicked, and that is foremost in our minds.
Quorum quidem exercitus tametsi numerosus est: Although their army is numerous,

tamen spernendus est: it is nevertheless to be despised. However great their host may be, it is still to be scorned. Quoniam nullo duce regitur: Because it is ruled by no leader. Because it is guided by no wise one. Sed raptatur tantum errore temere ac passim limphante: But it is only swept along by error, raving rashly and at random.

Instead, it is only driven here and there without counsel by raging error. Qui si quando struens aciem contra nos ualentior incubuerit: And if at any time it draws up its battle line and presses upon us in greater strength, nostra quidem dux contrahit copias suas in arcem: our leader draws her forces back into the citadel. If it also arrays its troops against us and attacks us in greater strength, then our leader, Virtue, draws her army into her fortress. Illi uero occupantur circa diripiendas inutiles sarcinulas: But they are kept busy plundering worthless bits of baggage. After that they keep themselves busy plundering our bundles [literally 'cushions']. This is what the men who killed Maurice did. When the virtue of faith drew him and the whole legion to heaven, they divided up the spoil. What could have mattered less to him then than what they were plundering? Therefore she says next:
At nos irridemus desuper rapientes uilissima quaeque rerum: But from above we laugh at them as they seize all the most worthless things.

But we, from above, hold those who snatch at such bad things in scorn. Secure from all the raging tumult. Become secure from all the raging storm. And fortified by that rampart, to which raging folly may not approach. And protected by that stronghold, to which raging foolishness has no way.
WHAT PRODUCES CONSTANCY.
Whoever, serene, with his life well ordered, has put proud fate beneath his feet,

that is, prosperous fortune, and, looking upright, that is, has rightly regarded both kinds of fortune: whoever in his lifetime was calm and disciplined and held good fortune in contempt, and rightly despised both, I mean good fortune and misfortune,
he could keep his face unconquered. He could keep a steady bearing. Socrates, for example, never changed his expression, because he was always the same, without laughter and without sadness.
The rage and threats of the sea will not move him

as it stirs up and churns its surge from the bottom. The unruliness and threats of the sea, seething and turning up its surge from the bottom, shall not disturb him. These are the tumults of worldly men. Nor will Vesuvius move him
whenever its furnaces burst open and it hurls its smoking fires far and wide.

Nor will the burning mountain Vesuvius, which is in Campania, disturb him, when it bursts open its vents and scatters its smoking fires far and wide. These are the furies of princes. Nor the path of the burning thunderbolt,
which often strikes lofty towers.
Nor will the shot of the fiery lightning bolts, which often strike down high towers, disturb him. That is the power of kings, which often deposes the mighty.
Why do the wretched, that is, the foolish, marvel so much at savage tyrants
who rage without strength? What is wrong with the wretched, that they fear the powerful? These are powerless, even though they rage.
Hope for nothing and fear nothing,

and you will have disarmed the anger of the powerless one, that is, the very powerful one. Follow my advice. Do not expect to gain anything, and do not fear to lose anything; in this way you take his anger away from the powerful man.
But whoever trembles in fear or desire,
because he is not steadfast and not his own master,
has thrown away his shield,

that is, the strength of the Lord's protection. But whoever will not do this, and fears to lose or desires to gain, because he is unsteady and has no power over himself, has thrown away his shield, that is, firmness of mind and trust in God. And, driven from his place, he fastens on the chain by which he can be dragged off. Driven from his position, as happens to the defeated man in battle, he forges for himself a chain with which he can be bound.
THAT A WOUND SHOULD NOT BE HIDDEN.
"Do you perceive these things," she said, that is, these songs, "and do they sink into your mind?"

"Do you understand any of this," she said, "or does it get into you at all? Does what I sing to you reach you at all? Ananos liras [Greek, garbled: ?], that is, one with no skill at the lyre, why do you weep? Wretched one, who has forgotten how to play the lyre, why do you weep? Why do you flow with tears? Exomologese, that is, confess; me ecripse ien [Greek, garbled: ?], that is, do not hide a single thing. Say what is wrong with you; do not hide a single thing. If you expect the physician's help, uncover the wound. If you want to be healed and want the physician's help, then show the wound."

THE SICK MAN TRIES TO REVEAL WHAT ILLNESS HE SUFFERS FROM. Then I: Then I answered her. Having gathered my mind into strength, that is, having gathered the strength in my mind: with somewhat stronger courage. Does it still need reminding? Does it still need to be said? Does the harshness of fortune raging against us not stand out clearly enough by itself? Does the misfortune that lies upon me not show itself well enough? Does the very appearance of the place not move you at all? Does the very dreadfulness of the prison not move you?
Is this the library that you yourself had chosen as your fixed seat in our house? Is this, then, now the book-chamber where you liked to sit, in my house? In which, often sitting with me,

you discoursed on the knowledge of divine and human things. And sitting together with me, you considered all the wisdom that concerns God and that concerns people. Was this my bearing, was this my face, when I searched out the secrets of nature with you? Was I in these clothes when I helped you look into the secret of nature, that is, questions of physics? When you traced out for me with a rod, that is, a staff, the paths of the stars, that is, the planets. When you drew for me in the dust, with your pointer, the courses of the seven wandering stars. Philosophers had a board in front of them, which they called a mensa (table); some called it an abacus. It was strewn with glassy dust, finely ground and carefully moistened, and they sat with their rod in hand,

and with it they drew for their pupils, in that same dust, the courses of the stars and all the figures that one must learn in geometry. An abacus is a descriptio, that is, a drawing on a board or on a page, as we see it now in our own times, where characters of various shapes are laid out, as on the board where people play at dice-tables (backgammon). With these characters the divisions and multiplications of all numbers are quickly worked out, whichever of them one needs, in music or in arithmetic. That discipline is called mathematics. When you formed our morals and the whole plan of our life after the pattern of the heavenly, that is, the angelic, order. When you shaped my ways and the whole manner of my life after the likeness of the angels. For this is why Christ, the wisdom of God, came here into the world: to teach people

to lead the angelic life on earth. To this end the philosophers taught ethics, that is, the discipline of morals. Are these the rewards we get for obeying you? Do I now have such a reward for heeding you?

HE EXCUSES HIS AMBITION. And yet you laid down, that is, established, this principle through the mouth of Plato. Truly, you found that saying and taught it through Plato's mouth: that commonwealths would be happy if either lovers of wisdom ruled them, or if their rulers happened to study wisdom. All kingdoms and all other powers would then be happy if their rulers were wise, or were people who applied themselves to wisdom. Solomon was wise; and Darius attached himself to Daniel the wise, and Pharaoh to Joseph. Through the mouth of the same man you warned that this reason for taking part in public affairs was necessary for the wise. Through his mouth you also taught us that it is useful for all wise men to gain power, in these words:
So that the helm of cities, if left to wicked and shameful citizens,

would not bring plague (that is, scandals) and ruin (that is, death) upon the good. So that it would not, left in the hands of the wicked, cause harm and destruction to the good. Following this authority, therefore — following it because it came from you — I chose to carry over into the work of public administration what I had learned from you in private leisure. I wanted to show in office what you had taught me in private.
You and God, who placed you in the minds of the wise, are witnesses

(supply: "are"). You bear witness for me, and so does God, who placed you in the wise, that I brought no aim to the magistracy except the common aim of all good men. You know I cared about nothing in the office (I mean the consulship) except the common good. From this came serious and implacable quarrels with the wicked. From that arose strong enmities against me from wicked men, which no one could settle. And, as freedom of conscience brings with it, I always scorned giving offence to the powerful in order to defend what was right. And, as the boldness of a clear conscience always does, for the love of right the anger of the powerful meant nothing to me.

HE RECALLS HIS WORKS OF DUTY AND GOODNESS. How often did I check (that is, prevent) Conigastus when he attacked the fortunes of any weak person? How often did I stop Conigastus the Goth when he went after the property of weak men! How often did I throw down Triguilla, overseer of the royal household, from an injustice he had begun and had in fact already carried out? How often did I push the count of the palace, Triguilla, away from his injustice, which he had begun and had even completed!

How often did I use my authority to protect the wretched, whom the unpunished greed of the barbarians (that is, the Goths) constantly harassed with endless false accusations? How often did I use my standing to defend the poor, whom the greed of the heathens troubled with impunity through countless injuries!
No one ever drew me away from right to wrong.

No man ever turned me from right to wrong. When the fortunes of the provincials were ruined, sometimes by private plunder and sometimes by public taxes, I grieved over it no less than those who suffered it. Not only the townspeople's property: when I also saw the country people's property ruined, whether because of the lord's tax or otherwise through someone's violent seizure, it weighed on me as heavily as on those who suffered it.
When, in a time of bitter famine, the praetorian prefect appeared to have decreed a heavy and unaccountable compulsory purchase that would have ruined the province of Campania through poverty,

(supply: when the king's granaries were opened). When, in years of severe famine, the king decreed a harsh sale of grain in Campania, one hard to pay for, which would have impoverished that population. I took up the fight against the praetorian prefect for the sake of the common good. Then I undertook to fight over it against the overseer of the praetorium, whose office it was, for the sake of the common need. I contended while the king heard the case. I contended with the knowledge of the king, whose grain it was. And I won: the purchase was not exacted. And I brought it about that no one forced them to make the purchase. Paulinus, a man of consular rank,
whose wealth the palace dogs had already devoured in their hope and ambition, I dragged from the very jaws of those gaping for it. Paulinus, an honourable [?] man, a consul,

whose goods the courtiers had already swallowed up, as far as their expectation and their greed went, I drew out of the throats of the gaping ones. So that the punishment of an accusation already judged in advance should not seize Albinus, a man of consular rank, I set myself against the hatred of the informer Cyprian. So that Albinus, a man of equal rank, should not be condemned without trial because he had been denounced, I set myself against the hatred of his accuser Cyprian. Do I seem to have stirred up,
that is, to have multiplied against myself, enmities that are great enough?

Does it not seem to you that I have stirred up enough enmities against myself? But I ought to have been safer with the others, that is, with the senate. Now I ought to be all the safer on the side of the others. For love of justice I kept nothing in reserve with the courtiers by which I might be safer. For love of justice I had protected myself all the worse against the courtiers.
THAT HE OUGHT NOT TO BE ACCUSED BY PERSONS OF UNPROVEN CHARACTER. But by what informers have we been struck down? By which accusers have I now been brought into distress?
Of these, Basilius, who had once been dismissed from the royal service, was driven by the pressure of his debts to inform against our name.

This Basilius, long since thrust out of the king's service, was induced to denounce me by the pressure of the money that he owed. He freed himself by doing so. Money that one person was obliged to pay to another was called aes alienum in Rome. But when the royal judgment had decreed that Opilio and Gaudentius should go into exile for countless and manifold frauds — when the king also ordered Opilio and Gaudentius to leave the country because of their many and manifold treacheries —

and when they, unwilling to obey, protected themselves by taking refuge in sacred buildings — and they fled into churches and would not obey the command — and when this became known to the king — and when the king came to know of it — he decreed
that if they did not leave the city of Ravenna within the appointed day, they should be branded on their foreheads and driven out. He commanded that if they did not leave Ravenna

before the deadline that he set them, they should be marked on the face and, thus marked, driven out. What could be added to this severity? And yet on that very day, on the information of these same men, the accusation against our name was accepted. What do you suppose could be said to win credence from the king's severity by those he was so angry with? And yet that same day he believed what they said about me. What then? What now, lady? Is this what my skills deserved? Is this what my virtues, which I displayed, have earned? Or did their earlier condemnation make them just accusers? Did their earlier condemnation make them lawful accusers?
Was Fortune not ashamed at all? Is Fortune so shameless? If she was not ashamed of the innocence that was accused,

she should at least have been ashamed of how low the accusers were. If she did not hold back out of respect for my innocence, why did the accusers' disgrace not seem shameful to her? But of what crime are we accused? What, then, are my offences?
REFUTATION OF THE CHARGES. Do you ask the sum of it? Do you want to know the main point? We are said to have wanted the senate to be safe. They accuse me of wanting to see the Roman senate kept safe.
Do you want the manner of it? Do you want to know how?
We are accused of having hindered an informer from delivering documents with which he would make the senate guilty of treason. They accuse me of having hindered the informer in this,

so that he would not bring the king the letters with which he would have made the senate guilty of a capital crime. A capital crime is plotting against the ruling power. The Roman senate wanted to complain by letters to the emperor, to whose good faith Theodoric had entrusted the land and the people, that he had taken their liberty from them. For this reason the king held Boethius himself and other senators guilty of treason. What then do you think, mistress? What do you make of it, mistress? Shall we deny the charge, so as not to bring shame on you? Shall I deny it, so that I am not found out in guilt and a dishonour to you? But I did want the senate to be safe.

Certainly I wanted that. Nor will I ever stop wanting it. I wanted it then, I want it now, and I always will. We will confess it. That I confess. But the effort stopped, that is, I made no effort to hinder the informer. In fact I did not hinder the informer. I would have done well if I had hindered him, but I did not hinder him in it. The first I confess; the second I do not. Shall I call it a crime to have wished for the safety of that order, that is, the senatorial order? Shall I count it wrong that I want to see those who belong to that order kept safe? Indeed that order had, by its decrees about me, that is, by making me consul, made it so that this would be a crime. It bound me by its appointment, that is, by appointing me to the consulship, so that it would be forbidden for me not to want to see them kept safe.
But folly, which always lies to itself, cannot change the merits of things,

that is, of deeds. But folly, lying to its own harm, can never overturn the truth with lies, nor the merits of deeds. It can never turn me from innocent into guilty. Nor do I think it right for me, by the Socratic decree, that is, judgment, either to have hidden the truth or to have admitted a lie. Nor do I think I am allowed, by the teaching of Socrates, to conceal the truth or to confess to a lie.
But however that may be, I leave it to be weighed by your judgment and that of the wise. But all of it, however it may be, and however guilty I am in it, I leave to your judgment,

and to that of the wise. I have committed the course and the truth of this matter to writing and to memory, so that it cannot be hidden even from those who come after. I have also written down the truth of this same deed in order, so that our descendants may learn of it too.
LIKEWISE. For what point is there in speaking of the forged letters by which I am accused of having hoped for Roman liberty? What do I now have to say about the lying letters?

...with which they accuse me of wanting to win back from the emperor the Roman self-rule? Roman self-rule consisted in this: that no one should do anything beyond what the senate agreed on. That agreement was called a senatus consultum (decree of the senate). Because Theodoric had taken it from them, and it weighed on them, they were out of his favour. Quarum fraus aperta patuisset: "Their fraud would have been laid open." The deceit of those letters would easily have come to light; people would easily have found out who wrote them. Si licuisset nobis uti confessione ipsorum delatorum: "If we had been allowed to use the confession of the accusers themselves." If only I had been allowed to face the charges of those who accuse me of it! Quod in omnibus negotiis maximas vires habet: "Which has the greatest force in all matters." That is the strongest thing in all matters, I mean being allowed to come face to face. Nam quae reliqua libertas potest sperari? "For what other liberty can be hoped for?" Since we may not even plead face to face, what liberty can we hope for beyond that? Atque utinam esset ulla: "And would that there were any!" Would to God we had any. Now there is none of it.

Respondissem verbo Canii: "I would have answered with the words of Canius." If I could come face to face with those who accuse me of having worked for this, I would answer them with the answer of Canius. Qui cum a Gaio Caesare, filio Germanici, diceretur conscius fuisse contra se factae coniurationis, "Si ego," inquit, "scissem, tu nescisses": "When Gaius Caesar, son of Germanicus, said that he had known of a conspiracy made against him, he said: 'If I had known, you would not have known.'" When Gaius accused him of knowing about the conspiracy that had been made against him, he said: "If I had known of it, it would have been hidden from you."
WHY GOD CONSENTS TO THE WICKED. Qua in re non ita hebetavit maeror sensus nostros: "In this matter grief has not so dulled my senses..."

Despite all these troubles, sorrow has still not taken over my mind so much or thrown it so far off course. Ut querar impios moliri scelerata contra virtutem: "...that I should complain that the impious plot crimes against virtue." That it should seem lamentable to me that wicked men hurry to ruin the virtuous. Sed effecisse quae speraverunt vehementer admiror: "But that they have accomplished what they hoped for, I greatly wonder at." But that they can succeed in what they hurry toward, that astonishes me. Nam velle deteriora fortasse fuerit nostri defectus, i[d est] interitus: "For to want worse things may perhaps be our failing, that is, our ruin." An evil will may perhaps be our ruin. Posse contra innocentiam quae sceleratus quisque conceperit, inspectante deo, simile est monstri: "But that every wicked man should be able to carry out against the innocent whatever he has thought up, while God looks on, is like a monstrous thing." But that, with God looking on, an evil man can act out his wicked will on the good, that is like something horrifying. That we have evil wills is harm to ourselves. That God also allows it to harm the good, that is a wonder.

Unde haud iniuria quaesivit quidam familiarium tuorum: "Si quidem deus est," inquit, "unde mala? Bona vero unde, si non est?" "Hence one of your followers asked, not without reason: 'If there is indeed a God,' he said, 'where do evils come from? And where do good things come from, if there is not?'" Therefore one of your close followers rightly asked: "Where," he said, "does evil come from, if God exists? And if he does not exist, where does the good come from?"

EVIL RETURNED TO HIM FOR GOOD. Sed fas fuerit nefarios homines, qui petunt sanguinem omnium bonorum totiusque senatus, nos quoque perditum ire voluisse, quos viderant propugnare bonis senatuique: "But let it be granted that wicked men, who seek the blood of all good men and of the whole senate, wanted to destroy me too, whom they had seen fighting for the good and for the senate." Now let the wicked, who would gladly destroy all good men and the whole senate, also be free to destroy me gladly, because I always stood by them.
Sed num idem de patribus merebamur? "But did I deserve the same from the senators?" Have I also deserved this same treatment from the senate?

Meministi, ut opinor, quoniam ipsa semper praesens me dirigebas dicturum quid vel facturum: "You remember, I think, since you yourself were always there to guide me whenever I was about to say or do anything." I think you remember it well.

that you yourself taught me all that I was to do and to say. How then could I have done wrong? "You remember," I said. You remember well. When the king at Verona, eager for the ruin of all, was striving to shift the charge of treason brought against Albinus onto the whole order of the senate. When the king at Verona wanted to turn one man's capital charge against the whole body of lords, willing to spare no one. With how little regard for my own danger I defended the innocence of the whole senate. With what confidence, and with what disregard for my own peril, I defended the innocence of the whole body of lords.
You know that I am saying these things truly, and that I have never boasted of them in any praise of myself.

You know that I am telling the truth, and that I never boasted for the sake of praise. For the secret of a conscience that approves itself (that is, its merit; that is, of one praising himself) is in some way lessened whenever someone, by displaying a deed, receives the reward of fame. I know well that the joy of a confident heart fades when it boasts of its deed and receives praise for it. But you see what outcome has befallen our innocence. Now you see well how my blamelessness has turned out for me. Instead of the rewards of true virtue, we suffer the punishments of a false crime. In return for my loyalty I pay the price of innocence and of a false ill report, namely that I am guilty of treason. And of what crime did a plain confession ever
find judges so agreed in severity that neither the very error of human understanding moved some of them, that is, inclined them to mercy,

nor the condition of fortune, which is uncertain for all? And who ever saw judges so united in mercilessness against someone who had actually been found guilty, that not one of them thought that charges can easily deceive the judge, or that he himself does not know what will happen to him? If we were said to have wanted to set fire to sacred buildings, to slaughter priests with an impious sword, to have plotted death for all good men. If I were accused of wanting to burn churches, slay priests, and take the lives of all good people. Even then, a sentence would have punished me only when I was present and had confessed or been convicted. Even then it would be right that a just sentence should be passed on me only if the matter came before me in person, and I confessed guilt and was convicted. Now, removed far away (from the city)

by nearly five hundred thousand paces. Now brought from Rome to Pavia, nearly five hundred miles away, into exile. And undefended. And no one allowed me to defend myself. Because of too eager a zeal for the senate, we are condemned to death and proscription. Because of the great love I showed the senate, I am condemned to death and to the confiscation of my goods. At Rome a man was called proscriptus when he was porro, that is, 'far', 'written' from his goods. When it was written over to the treasury, it was far from him. O, that no one can deservedly be convicted of a similar charge! Alas, all too much, that no one can any longer rightly be convicted of such guilt. Even the very men who brought the charge saw the honour of this offence. The informers themselves recognized it as an honourable guilt.
HE CLEARS HIMSELF OF THE SUSPICION OF SACRILEGE. In order to darken this by mixing in some crime,
they lied that I had defiled my conscience with sacrilege.

That is, necromancy, out of ambition for office. To disgrace that with yet another ill repute, they accused me, for love of office, of having defiled my mind with sorcery. And yet you, implanted in us, drove every desire for mortal things from the seat of our mind, and it was not lawful for sacrilege to have any place under your eyes. Truly, both are true:

both that you, dwelling within me, took from me all worldly desire, and that it was therefore impossible for me to let wickedness come near me while you were watching. For you instilled daily into my ears and my thoughts that saying of Pythagoras: "epi ov theon" [?]. You taught me daily what the philosopher Pythagoras said about things that are not sacred, or about those that are not gods. If they are not sacred, then they are sacrilegious; if they are not gods, then they are demons.
Nor was it fitting for me to seek the help of the vilest spirits, me whom you were shaping to such excellence as to make me like God.

How should I seek the help of the cast-out devils, since you have raised me to likeness with God? Man is created in the image and likeness of God. He is similar to Him, not equal; that is, alike, not of equal measure. Because the evil angel wished to make himself equal to Him, he was therefore cast out. Hence it is not permitted that man should forsake God, as those do who practise necromancy or any magical illusions, that is, sorcery, and invite unclean spirits to his help. Moreover, the inner chamber, that is, the secret place or bedchamber, which is to be understood as the wife: and besides that, my wife, the daughter of Symmachus. An innocent house, that is, household: and my sinless household. A gathering of most honourable friends: and all my most virtuous friends.

Also my holy father-in-law: and my God-fearing father-in-law Symmachus. And equally venerable in his very deeds: and just as worthy of honour in his conduct, for he shows by his deeds what he is. They defend us from all suspicion of this crime: these [?] clear me well of this charge.

HE GRIEVES THAT HIS TEACHER IS DEFAMED IN HIM. But oh, the wickedness! But alas, to my sorrow! They, however, draw from you belief in so great a crime: they suspect you of such guilt. And by this very fact we shall seem to have been party to the crime, that we are steeped in your teachings and trained in your ways: and in this very thing I seem to them a sorcerer, that I am acquainted with your arts and brought up according to your customs.

So it is not enough that reverence for you has profited me nothing, unless you in turn are torn apart by my offence: in this way it does not seem enough to them that I can gain nothing from your being venerable, unless you are dishonoured on my account, through me.
ON THE UNJUST OPINION OF THE WRETCHED. But this heap is added on top of our ills: this too piles itself upon the other sorrow. That the judgement of most people does not look at the merits of things!

...but the outcome of fortune. That is, the opinion of many does not turn to the merit of deeds, but to the outcome of deceptive good fortune. And it judges only those things to have been wisely foreseen which good fortune has commended. And it supposes there to be prudence only where success follows. By that they want to judge things, as Job's three friends wanted to. From this it comes about that good repute is the first of all things to abandon the unfortunate. From this it happens that good esteem is the first of all to give up those who have met with misfortune.
What rumors among the people now, how discordant and manifold their opinions,

it irks me to recall. For what reputation there now is about me among the people, how varied and how manifold the talk, who could bear to dwell on that? This only I would say: that the last burden of adverse fortune is this. I will only call this the sorest grief in misfortune: that when a charge is fastened on the wretched, they are believed to have deserved what they endure. When some guilt is smeared upon those who have been thrust into distress, people at once consider them deserving of what they suffer.

ON THE UNJUST CHANGE OF THINGS. And I indeed, driven from all my goods, stripped of my dignities, befouled in my reputation, have suffered punishment for a kindness. What more is there to say? Driven from my property, put out of office, besmirched with ill repute, I suffer injuries in return for good deeds.
But I seem to see the wicked workshops of criminals

overflowing with joy and gladness. It seems to me that I now see the dwellings of all the wicked overflowing with delight and joy. And every most abandoned man pressing on with new frauds of accusation. And each of the lost lying in wait, to see how, coming forward with new lies, he may denounce someone. The good lie prostrate with terror at my peril. The good do not dare to lift up their heads, terrified by my dangers. Every scoundrel is spurred on by impunity to dare a crime, and by rewards to carry it out. And every wicked man grows bold in evil because he goes unpunished, and is eager to accomplish it for the sake of reward.
But the innocent are deprived not only of security but even of defense itself. The innocent are deprived of all security
and even of every defense. Therefore I am moved to cry out. Now I will cry out about it to God.
THAT ONLY THE ACTS OF MEN ARE DISREGARDED BY GOD. O creator of the star-bearing sphere. You creator of heaven. HE DECLAIMS.
Who, resting on an everlasting throne,
turn the heaven in a swift whirl. You who are ever seated firmly turn that same heaven with a swift turning.
And compel the stars to submit to law.
And command the stars to keep their law. So that the moon, now bright with full horn,
facing all the flames of her brother,
hides the lesser stars,
now pale with darkened horn,
nearer to Phoebus, loses her light. So exactly that the moon at times, going full opposite the sun, darkens the other stars; but at other times, horned and waning, goes nearer to the sun.
And Hesperus, who drives on the chill risings at the time of early night,
again changes his accustomed reins,

pale as Lucifer at the rising of Phoebus. And also the evening star, which at times rises as night comes on and shines in the cool of the evening, changes his course in turn, rising toward day, and becomes the morning star.
You confine the light to a shorter stay in the cold of leaf-shedding winter. In winter, when the leaves fall, you make the day shorter
than the night. When hot summer has come,
you divide the swift hours for the night. But on the other hand, when it becomes hot in summer, you give fewer hours to the night than to the day.
Your power tempers the changing year. You temper the year; by your power you make it varied.
So that the leaves which the breath of Boreas, the north wind, takes away,
gentle Zephyrus brings back. So that the west wind brings back the leaves that the north wind takes away.
And the seeds which Arcturus saw,

Sirius burns as tall crops. And the grain that is sown in autumn, when Arcturus rises with the sun, ripens in summer, when Sirius rises with the sun. Arcturus is a star in the sign of Boötes; the other, Sirius, is in the tongue of the Greater Dog.
Nothing, released from the ancient law,
leaves the work of its proper station. Nothing is lawless, and nothing wishes to leave its place.
Ruler, governing all things toward a fixed end,
you refuse only the acts of men
to restrain in due measure. O God, you hold all things under constraint, yet you do not wish to force the deeds of men to what is right for them. Where would free will be, then, if he forced them?
For why does slippery Fortune bring about such great changes?
Harmful punishment, owed to crime,

weighs on the innocent. How is it that Fortune brings about such unjust changes? The harm that should fall on the guilty lies upon the innocent. But wicked conduct sits on the lofty throne. Wicked people sit in the foremost places.
And the harmful, by an unjust turn, trample on holy necks. And harmful people tread the necks of the saints underfoot, by an unjust change.
Shining virtue lies hidden, concealed in dark shadows. Virtue, which was always bright, lies hidden in the darkness. Those who are openly virtuous hide themselves.
And the just man has borne the crime of the unjust. The righteous man swears to the guilt of the unjust [?].
Perjuries do not harm them,
and deceit does not harm them, decked in lying colours, that is, adorned with hypocrisy. Perjuries do not harm them, nor does faithlessness covered by pretence.
But when they please to use their strength,
they delight in bringing down the highest kings,

that is, certain perfect men who rule their own conduct. When they then want to test what they are able to do, they attack the mightiest kings, such as those whom no one can turn from what is right. They press them to give way and go over to their side. Whom countless peoples fear. Whom many people fear, that is, because of their just judgments.
O you, whoever you are, who bind the bonds of things together, look now upon the wretched lands. O you who create the unity of all things, remember the wretched who are on earth.
We men, no worthless part of so great a work!
are tossed on the sea of fortune. We, who are a great part of your excellent work,

we struggle in this sea of fortune, that is, of the changeableness of time. Ruler, restrain the raging waves. Calm, O ruler, the perilous billows. And make firm the steady lands, that is, men, with the bond
by which you rule the immense heaven,
that is, the angels, or the stars. And with the same peace with which you govern the heavenly things, so govern the earthly. Make peace as steadfast on earth as it is in heaven.
WHAT TRUE EXILE IS, AND WHERE THE TRUE FATHERLAND IS.

When I had barked out these things in unbroken grief, she, with a calm face and not at all moved by my complaints, said: When I had thus cried out in unceasing pain, she spoke with a kindly look, and not angered by my complaint.
When I saw you sad and weeping, I knew at once that you were wretched and an exile.

That is, removed from reason. When I first saw you sad and weeping, I knew at once that you were wretched and in exile. But I did not know how far away that exile was, until your speech revealed it. But I would not have known how far that exile was, if your speech had not shown it to me. But you have not been driven so far from your fatherland; rather, you have strayed. Yet you have not been driven far from home, but have wandered off and gone astray. But if you would rather be thought to have been driven out, then you have expelled yourself. If you also want to call yourself driven out, it was you yourself who did it to yourself. You have driven yourself out. For no one would ever have been permitted to do this to you. No one else could have done it.
For if you remember of what fatherland you are a native, it is not ruled by the government of the multitude, as that of the Athenians once was. If you want to know

where you were born: there no multitude rules, as happened long ago at Athens, when the Lacedaemonians, their enemies, had set thirty lords over them. Read Orosius; he will tell you about it. But there is one lord, one king. Rather, there is one lord there and one king, who rejoices in a great number of citizens, not in their banishment. He would rather gather his townspeople together than drive them out. To be guided by his reins, that is, to be subject to his discipline, and to obey justice, is the highest freedom. Whoever serves him and is subject to him is fully free.
Or do you not know that most ancient law of your city, by which it is decreed that whoever has chosen to found his dwelling in it may not be exiled? Do you not know how it is laid down

in the law of the city in which you were born? Whoever wishes to build his dwelling there shall not be made an outcast. For whoever is enclosed by its rampart and fortification, whoever dwells inside it, fenced in and fortified, need have no fear that he will deserve to be an exile. He does not fear exile.
But whoever ceases to wish to dwell in it equally ceases to deserve it as well. But whoever has no desire to dwell in it does not strive to earn it either.

THE REPLY TO WHAT CAME BEFORE. So the look of this place does not move me as much as your own face does. Now the sight of this prison does not trouble me as much as your face does. Nor do I miss the walls of your library, adorned with ivory and glass, as much as the seat of your mind. Nor do I ask for the decorated walls of your book-chamber, with their ivory and glass, as gladly as I ask for the dwelling place of your mind. There, not books, but what gives books their value,
I once placed the thoughts of my books.

There I once placed what stands in the books, the worth of the books, not the books themselves. And you have indeed spoken truly about your services to the common good, but you have said little, given how many things you did. You have said little about the good you have done for the public, compared to what is true.
About whether the charges against you are honourable or false, you have recalled things known to everyone.

You spoke of the chaste deed they accuse you of, and of the lies, which are known to all. About the crimes and frauds of the informers, you rightly thought they should be touched on only briefly. You think it right that you should say little about their wicked crimes and treacheries. Because these things are better and more fully spread by the mouth of the common people, who recognize everything. Because all the people, to whom these things are well known, speak of them better and more fully. You also strongly rebuked the deed of the unjust senate. You have very harshly reproached the senate for its unjust judgment.
You also grieved over the charges against us. You also complained that they accuse me. You also wept for the loss of your damaged reputation.

You also lamented the dishonour of your bad reputation. Finally your grief flared up against Fortune. Lastly you quarrelled with Fortune. And you complained that rewards are not weighed out equal to merits. And you complained that you were unjustly rewarded. At the end of your raging Muse, that is, as you murmured against God, you set down prayers that the peace which rules heaven might also rule the earth. In those angry verses you prayed at the end for peace on earth as in heaven.

WHAT IS FIRST FITTING FOR ONE WHO IS GRAVELY ILL. But since a great tumult of passions has fallen upon you, and grief, anger and sorrow pull you in different directions. Since many impatient feelings now storm in your heart and turn you in many directions,
pain,

anger, sadness. In your present state of mind, stronger remedies cannot yet reach you, that is, it is not yet time for me to show you the highest good. As long as your mind is still like this, strong medicines will do you no good. So for a little while we will use gentler ones, that is, by first showing that Fortune is nothing. Now let us begin with gentler ones. So that what has hardened into a swelling from the inflow of disturbances may be softened by a gentler touch, ready to receive a sharper medicine. So that the swellings that have grown hard from the sorrows that attacked you may be softened with a gentle poultice, so as to endure stronger medicines.
A COMPARISON IS GIVEN.
He who has entrusted abundant seed to furrows that refuse it [gloss: THAT ORDER MUST BE KEPT IN MEDICINE], at the time when the heavy constellation of Cancer burns with the rays of Phoebus,
cheated by his trust in Ceres,
let him go to the oak trees. He who [does] so, when the sun in Cancer made its greatest heat,
[Whoever] sowed much in an unwilling field, because it was out of season, let him therefore go without grain to the wood, to the acorns, and feed himself on them.
When you are about to gather violets,
never, when the field has bristled, shrieking with the fierce north winds, seek the purple grove, that is, the violet-bed.

If you also want flowers when the field is bristling from the cold and roaring north wind, then do not go to the flower garden, where roses and marigolds and violets grow, which make the garden glow purple.
Nor, if it pleases you to enjoy grapes, should you seek in spring with greedy hand
to strip the vine-shoots.
Bacchus has rather bestowed his gifts on autumn. If you long for grapes, do not therefore think of handling the grapes in spring. God gave that honor to autumn, not to spring.
God marks the seasons,
fitting them to their proper offices. God has marked all the seasons and fitted them to their offices. Nor does he allow their turns to be mixed,
which he himself has restrained.
Nor does he let the alternations among them, which he himself has distinguished, be confused. Thus. As you have now heard.
Whatever by a headlong way abandons the fixed order
does not have happy outcomes. Whatever, while always going astray, believes itself to be right never comes out well in the end. Therefore I must treat you step by step; otherwise it cannot succeed.

PROBING OF THE WOUND. First, then. Now say first: will you allow me to touch you and test the state of your mind with a few small questions, so that I may understand what the manner of your cure should be? Will you allow me to feel you out by questioning and examine your mind, how it stands? So that I may know how I should heal you.
Ask, I said, at your own discretion whatever you wish, and I will answer.

According to your will, lady, I said, ask whatever you want me to answer. Then she said. Then she said: Do you think this world is driven by rash and fortuitous chances? Or do you believe there is in it some government of reason? Do you think these worldly events go on abandoned and haphazardly? Or do you think there is some rightness in them according to reason?
But, I said, I would by no means think that things so certain are moved by fortuitous rashness. Truly, I said, it would never come into my mind

that such certain things proceed by wavering unrightness. But I know that God the creator presides over his work. Rather, I know that God cares for his work. Nor will there ever be a day that drives me from the truth of this opinion. Nor will the day ever come that takes me away from this statement.
So it is, she said. That is so, she said. For you also sang this a little earlier. You sang that very thing before. And you lamented that men alone are without a share in divine care.

And you lamented that men alone are neglected by God. That was when he said: "Governing all things with a fixed end, you reject only the acts of men, O ruler, restraining in due measure." For about the rest you were not at all troubled that they were governed by reason. About the other things you were not angry [claiming] that they were not guided according to reason. Oh, but I wonder greatly why, set in so healthy an opinion, you are sick. And now I wonder greatly why, standing on so wholesome a view, you still waver.
But let us examine more deeply; I suspect something is lacking.

Let us search deeper. I do not know what it is, but it seems to me that you are lacking something. But tell me: since you do not doubt that the world is ruled by God, do you also perceive by what helm it is governed? Tell me now: since you know that God rules the world, do you know what he rules it with? With what rudder? She wanted to teach him that the prosperity and adversity of the world are its helms. "I scarcely understand the meaning of your question," I said, "much less can I answer what you ask." I do not even quite understand what you are asking. Much less could I answer you.
"Was I mistaken," she said, "that something was missing,

through which the sickness of disturbances has crept into your mind, as through a gap in the strength of a palisade?" "Did I not know well," she said, "that you were lacking somewhere, where sickness of mind can slip in, as through widely spaced stakes?" Where the Romans made camp, they dug a ditch around themselves and threw the earth inward, up against the ditch itself. On the mound by the ditch they set round, pointed stakes as close together as they could, so that no one could shoot through. That fence was called vallum; the stakes themselves were called valli; the gap between the stakes was called intervallum.

"But tell me, do you remember what the end of things is, or toward what the striving of all nature is directed?" Now tell me: do you remember what the end of all things is, and toward what all nature strives? She wanted him to say: toward the good. For God is the good; he is the end, just as he is also the beginning. "I had heard it," I said, "but grief has dulled my memory." "I knew it once," I said, "but now my memory of it has slipped away from me because of grief." "And yet
you know where all things came from." Truly, you do know where all things came from.
"I know," I said. "That I know." And I answered that it was God.

And I said at once that it was God. "And how can it be that, knowing the beginning, you do not know what the end of things is?" "And how can you," she said, "know the beginning and not know the end? But these disturbances of the mind are so strong that they can indeed move a man from his place, but tear him up
and root him out of himself entirely they cannot."

Sicknesses of the mind have the power to shake a person, like a tree standing in its place, but not to overturn him or uproot him. They can lead him astray in his understanding, but they cannot take it away from him entirely. "But I would also like you to answer this: do you remember that you are a human being?" But I would like you to tell me: do you know that you are a human being? "Why should I not remember?" I said. Why should I not know that? "Can you then set out what a human being is?" Can you then tell me what a human being is? "Is this what you are asking, whether I know that I am a rational and mortal animal?" Are you asking me whether I know myself to be, as Aristotle says,
a rational animal and mortal? "I know it,

and I acknowledge that I am that." That I know, and I declare that I am that. As I learned it in school, so I still remember it. And she said: And she again: "Do you remember that you are nothing else?" Do you not know, then, that you are anything else?

"Nothing." "No, I [know nothing more]." She wanted him to say that he, a man, was a god in God. "Now I know," she said, "another, indeed the greatest, cause of your sickness: you have ceased to know what you yourself are." "Now," she said, "I know the fitting [?] (stúreda) of your sickness, and a very powerful one too. You do not know the rudders of the world, nor the end of things; and what you yourself are, you have also given up knowing."
Therefore I have found out most fully both the reason for your illness and the way to restoring your health.

Therefore I have now understood well both how you are sick and how one should set about restoring you to your health. For since you are confounded by forgetfulness of yourself: because you have forgotten yourself, that is one thing. And you grieved that you were an exile and stripped of your own goods: and you lamented that you were exiled and robbed of your goods, that is the second.

[Heading, interwoven with the text:] ALTHOUGH HE IS GRAVELY ILL, HE IS NOT TO BE DESPAIRED OF. But since you do not know what the end of things is, you think worthless and wicked men are powerful and happy.
And since you have forgotten by what rudders the world is governed, you suppose that these changes of fortune drift about without a ruler.

These are great causes not only of sickness but even of death. Since you do not know the end of things, that is the third; and you think wicked people are mighty and blessed, that is the fourth; because you have also forgotten by what means God rules the world, that is the fifth; and you think the changes of passing fortune drift without a ruler, that is the sixth. Of these you have plenty, enough not only for sickness but for death. But thanks be to the author of health that nature has not yet wholly abandoned you. But thanks be to God, who gives health, that nature has not yet deprived you of all your sense.
We have the greatest kindling for your recovery: your true opinion about the governance of the world, that you do not believe it to be subject to the randomness of chance, that is, to random chances,

but to divine reason. In this true statement of yours about the governance of the world, that you do not think it subject to disorderly happenings but to God's wisdom, I have a spark of your recovery that is large enough. Therefore fear nothing; the vital warmth will soon shine upon you from this tiny spark. Take good comfort; living vigor will come to you from this little understanding.
But since it is not yet time for stronger remedies, and it is well established that the nature of minds is such that whenever they cast off true opinions they put on false ones,
and from these opinions there arises a darkness of disturbances that confuses that true sight, I shall try to thin this darkness a little with gentle and moderate poultices.

But because it is not yet time for stronger medicine, and the human mind is so made that as soon as it renounces the truth it immediately fastens onto false belief, from which comes the darkness of mental turmoil that confuses true sight, I shall first try to overcome that darkness with gentle and moderate poultices. So that, once the darkness of deceptive passions has been driven away, you may recognize the splendor of the true light. So that, when the darkness of false attachments of the mind has been removed, you may then see the true light.
Likewise it is shown by a simile [that] from the four passions darkness [?]. Stars hidden by black clouds
can [shed] no [?] … of minds to arise [?].
pour forth light.
Stars cannot shine when dark clouds are in front of them.
If the stormy south wind, rolling the sea,

stirs up the surge. If the wind also churns up the swell and makes the sea heave. Soon, once the mud is stirred up, the dirty water blocks the sight. As soon as it has turned muddy, the murky water resists the eyes.
Formerly glassy
and like
to clear days.
That which before was clear
and like bright days.
And the river flowing down, which wanders from high mountains. And the river running down from the mountain.
is often checked by the obstacle of a rock of loosened stone. It is often thrust back against the jutting crags
of the broken stones.
You too, if you wish to discern the truth in clear light. If you too wish to perceive the truth with clear eyes
and to take your path along a straight track. And to walk along the right way:
drive away joys,
drive away fear. So let your rejoicing be, let your fearing be.
And put hope to flight,
and let grief not be present.

Have no hope, have no grief. That is: do not rejoice over good fortune at hand; do not fear misfortune ahead; do not hope to gain something in the future; do not grieve at having lost something at hand. These are the four fetters of the mind: joy, hope, fear, grief. Virgil also mentions them. Two of them concern the present, two the future. Of these same things Cicero said that whichever of them is upon a man, he cannot be a just judge. Following this, she now says: The mind where these reign is clouded
and bound with reins.
The mind that these rule is murky and fettered. HERE ENDS THE FIRST BOOK OF BOETHIUS ON THE CONSOLATION OF PHILOSOPHY.

HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK OF BOETHIUS. WHAT THE CAUSE OF THE SICKNESS IS. After this she was silent for a little while. After this she kept silent a little. And when she had gathered my attention by her modest silence. And when, from my disciplined silence, she perceived my attentiveness, that is, how closely I listened to her,

she began thus. Thus she began: If I have fully understood the causes and condition of your sickness. If I have rightly understood where your sickness came from, what kind it is, and what ails you: you are wasting away with longing for your former fortune. So you are wasting away with resentment over your former good fortune, which you long for. Its change, as you imagine it to yourself, has so greatly perverted your mind. Changed, as you think, it has so severely overthrown your mind, that is, compared with what it would be if it were constant. I understand the many-shaped disguises of that monster. I recognize all the deceptive images of that monster.

And [she feigns] a most flattering familiarity with those whom she strives to deceive. And how charmingly she makes herself familiar with those whom she means to deceive. Until she confounds with unbearable grief those whom she has unexpectedly abandoned. Until, with bitter pain, she throws into confusion the minds of those whom she unexpectedly deserts.

THAT FORTUNE IS TO BE DETESTED EVEN WHEN SHE FLATTERS. If you recall her nature, her ways and what she deserves, you will recognize that you neither had anything beautiful in her nor have lost it. And if you will remember her nature, and her ways, and what she has deserved of you and of everyone, then you will see that you had nothing delightful in her then, nor have lost anything since. But, as I think, I shall not have to labor much to recall these things to your memory. I do not think either that I need to struggle very much

to remind you of this. For you used to attack her with manly words even when she was present and flattering you. You were also accustomed at that time to rebuke her with manly words, while she was serving you and caressing you. And bringing forth sayings, you drove her out of our sanctuary. And with old sayings you chased her out of our dwellings. You remembered the saying: 'There is change in all things.' And this one: 'The last things do not answer to the first in the same order.'
But every sudden change of things does not happen without a certain surging, as it were, of minds.

Yet no sudden overthrows of things happen without some agitation of minds. So it has happened that you too have fallen away a little from your tranquility. From that it has come about that you too have been moved somewhat away from your equanimity.

ON THE REMEDIES TO BE APPLIED FIRST. But it is time for you to take in and taste something soft and pleasant.
