But now it is time for you, since you are so sick, to drink something mild and sweet, and now, first of all, to taste it. Which, having passed into the inner parts, may make way for stronger draughts. That, swallowed beforehand, may make way for stronger drinks, that is, antidotes.

Let the persuasion of rhetorical sweetness therefore be present. Now let rhetoric help here with her sweet persuasion. Which proceeds on the right path only then. Which goes rightly only then. When she does not abandon our precepts. When she does not step beyond my teaching. That is as if she said: All the disciplines are mine; I taught that in rhetoric one should persuade to what is good, what is just, what is honorable, what is useful, what is necessary, what is possible. Whoever does otherwise, persuading to what is evil, shameful, unjust, useless, unnecessary, impossible, turns rhetoric to evil,

that is, he abuses the art. Therefore it is written in rhetoric: 'An orator is a good man skilled in speaking.' If he is bad, even though he may be skilled in speaking, he is by no means an orator, but a seducer. Like the one who, persuading, said to you: 'You shall not die at all, but you shall be like gods.' Rhetoric can do great things. She converts people from falsehood to truth. She gives consolation to the sorrowful and faith to the unbelieving, and she makes the senseless sensible. Because this is so, she is therefore so close to philosophy; therefore she wishes to heal this sick man with her power. And let music sing along with her.

[Let Music,] a home-born servant of our house, [sing] now lighter, now heavier modes. And along with rhetoric, let music always be my housemate, and sing right after the prose: sometimes a heavier song, as the heroic metre is; sometimes a lighter one, as the iambic is; and other metres.

DESCRIPTION OF FORTUNE. What is it, then, O man, that has cast you down into sadness and grief? Come now, dear man, what has brought you to this state, into this sadness and into this weeping? You have seen, I believe, something new and unusual. Something, I do not know what, new and strange has befallen you. You think that Fortune has changed toward you. You think that Fortune has changed against you.

You are wrong. In that you err. These have always been her ways; this is her nature. These are her customs; that is how she is made. Rather, she has kept toward you her own constancy, in her very changeableness. She has shown you her steadiness more than ever, in her very changing. This is called argumentum a nota, that is, an explanation from the name. For what else is fortune but the changeableness of prosperity and adversity? Such she was when she flattered you. Such she was when she was most agreeable to you, when she caressed you. When she played up to you with the allurements of false happiness. Then she played with you with the lures of false happiness.
You have discovered the two-sided faces of the blind divinity.

Now you recognize the face of this hidden deceiving demon. Or say: of the blind goddess, because the ancients held her to be a goddess and painted her blind. Why blind? Because her giving is such as if she did not see to whom she gives. She gives to the worse and passes over the better. She who still veils herself from others has become wholly known to you. She who still hides herself from others has revealed herself to you. If you approve of her, make use of her ways. If she pleases you, put up with her ways. Do not complain. And do not lament. If you shudder at her faithlessness,

scorn and cast away her who plays so perniciously. If you loathe her faithlessness, then renounce her and cast her away, for she plays in an evil way. While she is still playing with you, keep away from her, before she fails you! For what is now the cause of such great grief to you ought to have been the cause of your peace of mind. What you now grieve over should have put you in good spirits. For she has left you. For she has now abandoned you. And no one can ever be sure that she will not leave him. She who never becomes certain for anyone.
Or do you really consider precious a happiness that is going to depart, that is, withdraw? Do you consider precious a fleeting happiness? And is present fortune dear to you,

which is neither faithful in staying and will bring grief when she departs? And should she be dear to you while she is with you, she who is with you without faithfulness and who at some time will grieve you by leaving you? But if she cannot be held at one's will, if no one can keep her according to his own will, and if by fleeing she makes people wretched; and she, going away, makes them sorrowful,
what else is a fleeting thing but a kind of sign of future calamity?

What is she, then, but fleeting, if she gives no sign of the sorrow to come? Such was Aeneas to Dido. That argument is called "ab eventu", that is, "from the end" or "from the effect", because we should look at the end within the deed that comes before it. As Virgil said: "While driving them, beware of running into the he-goat; he butts with his horn." Nor would it be enough to look at what lies before the eyes. Nor should anyone look only at what is before his eyes. Prudence measures the outcomes of things. Prudence considers the end of all things; she always thinks ahead. And the same changeability in either direction... And the same change in both, the good and the evil.
...makes neither the threats of fortune to be feared nor her caresses to be desired.
It does not let her, that is, prudence, fear the coming threats of fortune, nor love her present caresses.

A YOKE TAKEN UP FREELY MUST NOT BE BORNE IMPATIENTLY. Finally, once you have submitted your neck to her yoke, you must bear with an even mind whatever is done within the domain of fortune. Finally, if you once put your neck under her, you must bear with an even mind whatever is done to you in her court and whatever befalls you there. That is called "argumentum a coniugatis" (argument from related terms). Cicero gave this example of it: "If the field is a common pasture, it is lawful to graze it in common." That means: if the pasture is common, one must use it in common. This is like that: "If you subject yourself to the yoke,

you must bear the yoke." But if you wished to write a law of staying and a law of leaving for her whom you freely chose as your mistress, would you not be unjust? If you want to set a law for your mistress, whom you won of your own free will, about how long she is to stay with you, or even when she is to leave, are you not then dealing with her unfairly? And by impatience you would make the lot that you cannot change more bitter. And you would break against [?] the lot with impatience, that is, impatiently resent the fate that you cannot change. That is rhetorical dissuasion: never attempt what cannot be done.

If you committed your sails to the winds, you would move forward not where your will was aiming but where the gusts drove you. If you left your sail to the power of the wind, you would not travel where you wanted but where the wind carried you. If you entrusted seeds to the fields, you would weigh the fruitful years and the barren ones against each other. If you entrust your seed to the earth, you must of necessity take your chances with good years and bad. What was lacking in the bad year, you would make up with the good.
You have given yourself over to fortune to be ruled; you must obey the ways of your mistress.

You entrusted yourself to fortune so that she would take care of you; now follow her ways, for that is right. Those who are powerful in eloquence know how to bring forward such a pairing of paradigms, that is, of examples. For this reason rhetoric is also named among the Greeks from "copia fandi" (abundance of speech). But you are trying to hold back the force of the turning wheel? Are you striving to stop the spinning wheel that she drives? Yet, most foolish of all mortals, if she begins to stay, she ceases to be chance. Most foolish of men, if she begins to stand still, she is no longer changeable. That argument is called "a contrariis" (from contraries), because Aristotle says that motion is contrary to rest.
HOW MUCH SHE DOES WHILE SHE SHOWS HER STRENGTH. When she has turned the changes with her proud right hand,
She is swept along like the seething Euripus. And so when she overturns things with her proud right hand, she moves like the surging whirlpool. This figure is called parabole, that is, comparison.
Fierce, she tramples kings who were dreaded only a moment ago. And she cruelly tramples down the kings who were feared just a moment ago.
And, deceitful, she raises up the humbled face of the vanquished.
And on the other hand she deceitfully lifts up the head of the defeated. She does not hear or care about wretched weeping. She pays no heed at all to pitiful weeping.

And she even laughs at the groans that she, the hard one, has caused. And she gladly laughs at the sighing she has brought about. Through pride and cruelty she shows herself worthy of hatred, and through deceit worthy of contempt. This is what rhetoric teaches us to do to someone we want to make hateful to others.
So she plays; so she tests her strength. That is her game; in this way she tests what she can do.
And she shows her followers a great marvel:
if someone is seen in a single hour both cast down and happy. And she puts on this marvel for those who watch her: someone who, within one short while, becomes both happy and unhappy.

WHAT FORTUNE'S OWN ARGUMENT MIGHT BE. But I would like to discuss a few things with you in Fortune's own words. I would now gladly talk with you a little in her own words. So consider whether she is demanding what is right. Judge whether her demand is just.
Why, man, do you accuse me with your daily complaints?

Why must you [?] me every day with your complaints? What wrong have we done you? What wrong have I done you? What of your goods have we taken from you? What of your goods have I taken away from you? Contend with me before any judge you like about the possession of wealth and high offices. Sue me before whatever judge you wish about your goods and about your office. And if you show that any of these belongs as property to any mortal, I will now willingly concede that what you are reclaiming was yours. And if you show me any man who owns any of it as his own, I will also grant you what you demand. This argument is called 'from the genus', because what is the right of all is also the right of one. It proceeds from all to one. The status, that is, the legal dispute, is called 'absolute' in rhetoric,

as when the accused does not deny the deed but denies the guilt, and says: 'I rightly had to do so.' When nature brought you forth naked from your mother's womb, I took you up naked and lacking everything, and I nourished you with my riches. And what now makes you impatient with us is that, inclined to favour you, I brought you up too indulgently. When you were born naked, I took you in naked and destitute of everything, and fed you with my goods. And the reason you are now so resentful is that I gladly and willingly spoiled you.
I surrounded you with the abundance and splendour of everything that is mine to give.

I gave you plenty of everything that belongs to me, in abundance and in splendour. Now it pleases me to withdraw my hand. Now I want to draw my hand back to myself. You owe thanks, as one who has had the use of another's things. Now you owe me thanks for it, as one who enjoys another's goods. You have no right to complain, as though you had lost what was entirely your own. You have no just complaint, as though you had lost what was yours. Why then do you groan?

What are you sighing about, then? No violence has been done to you by us. I have taken nothing from you by force. Wealth, honors, and the rest of such things are under my authority. Riches and honor and things of that kind all belong to me. The servants know their mistress; they come with me, and when I go away they depart. They are my servants. They acknowledge me. They come together with me.

they depart together with me. This ornament of speech is called homoeoteleuton, that is, "similarly ended." Cicero, in the Rhetoric to Herennius, calls it similiter desinens ("ending similarly"), because it comes in a regular measure, like poetry. I would boldly affirm. I dare to say this boldly. If the things whose loss you complain of were yours, you would in no way have lost them. If what you say you have lost were yours, you would not have lost it; then it would not be foreign to you. This argument is called "from contraries" (a repugnantibus), because one's own and foreign are contraries. What anyone has by nature is his own; he cannot lose that. What he gains from outside is foreign; that he can lose.
Shall I alone be prevented from exercising my right?

May I alone, then, not show my power? This is indignation combined with rivalry, as Juno said of Minerva: "Could Pallas burn the fleet of the Argives and drown the men themselves in the sea?" The sky may bring forth bright days and hide them again in dark nights. The heaven may give bright days and dark nights by turns. The year may now crown the face of the earth with flowers and fruits, and now confound it with rain-clouds and cold. The year may by turns adorn the earth with plants and with grain, and at times also disfigure it with downpours and with frost. The sea [?] has the right now to charm with a calm surface, now to bristle with storms and waves. The sea too may be still at times, with a smooth, level surface, and at other times bristle up from the wind and from the waves.
Shall the insatiable greed of human beings bind us to a constancy that is foreign to our ways?

Shall the insatiable greed of human beings make me steadfast against my own nature? This is a rhetorical declamation, that is, reproach and rebuke, just as, on the other hand, acclamation means praise. This is our power; this is the game we play without ceasing. This is my power; this is the game I play. We turn the wheel in its revolving circle. I play with an ever-turning wheel; that is what I drive. We delight in changing the lowest to the highest and the highest to the lowest. I delight in turning what is low upward and what is high downward. Climb up, if it pleases you. Sit up there, if you like. But on this condition. But on these terms. Do not think
that is, that you do not think it an injury to come down when the rule of my game demands it.

That it should not seem a hardship to you to get down when my game turns that way. Or did you not know my ways? Were my habits not known to you? This is confutation, that is, shaming, as if she were saying: "If you are ignorant, I will make you wise." Did you not know that Croesus, king of the Lydians, who shortly before had been dreaded by Cyrus, then soon afterward became pitiable, was handed over to the flames of the pyre, and was saved by a rain sent from heaven? Do you not know that Croesus, who was king in Lydia,

…how he, who at that time was feared by Cyrus, soon afterwards became pitiable, and, thrown by him into the fire, was rescued by a downpour of rain? For Croesus came to help the Babylonians against Cyrus. From this it happened that he [Cyrus] drove him away from there, and soon after, pursuing him, captured him and threw him into the fire, from which God released him. But when he did not thank God for this, and boasted of his own good fortune, it happened that he dreamed he saw Jupiter pouring water over him and the sun wiping it off. His daughter interpreted the dream for him thus: that Cyrus would capture him again and hang him on the cross, and as the rain wet him, the sun would dry him; and so it afterwards came to pass.
Has it escaped you that Paulus shed pious tears over the calamities of King Perses, whom he had captured? Is it hidden from you

that the consul Paulus Aemilius piously wept over the misfortune of Perses, king of the Macedonians, whom he himself had captured, because he thought the same could happen to him? Historians call him Perseus, not Perses. They also tell how often he had defeated other consuls before, and, when Paulus brought him captive to Rome, how he died in custody, and how his son learned smithing out of poverty and supported himself by it. What else does the outcry of tragedies lament but Fortune overturning happy kingdoms with an indiscriminate blow? What do tragedies lament but Fortune heedlessly destroying glorious kingdoms, since she regards no one more than another? Tragedies are mournful poems, such as those Sophocles wrote among the Greeks about the overthrow of kingdoms and cities, and they are the opposite of comedies,

in which we always hear a joyful and pleasant ending. But we do not know whether any Latin tragedians are to be found, as we find plenty of Latin comic poets. Did you not learn as a youth that two jars lie on the threshold of Jupiter, [?] two jars, the one evil, the other good [?] [garbled Greek quotation]. Did you not learn, when you were a child, what the poet Pacuvius wrote: that two jars lie full beneath Jupiter's doors, one of good and the other of evil? Who is there that does not drink of both, that does not taste both hardship and comfort? By this she shows that she could not spare him adversity. What if you have taken more abundantly from the share of good things? Why do you complain if you have drunk more of the better? As if she were saying: if I could not spare you altogether, still I have not struck you too hard.
What if I have not departed from you entirely? What if I have not yet wholly abandoned you? What if this very changeableness of mine is a just cause for you to hope for better things?

What if this fall rightly makes you hope for something better? Just as all those rightly hope for something better who suffer persecution for righteousness' sake, because they are all the more blessed. Yet do not waste away in spirit. Now do not be so sick at heart; let go of your heartache. And since you have been placed within a kingdom common to all, do not wish to live by your own law. Do not desire to live alone by your own law in a common realm. Now she has come to the commonplace (communis locus). In any argument, a commonplace is when someone attacks vices common to all without naming anyone, as these verses do.
THE COMMONPLACE.
If Abundance were to pour out from her full horn as much wealth as the sea, stirred up by the winds, churns grains of sand,

What more is there? Suppose Abundance (Copia), the handmaid of Fortune, were to shake out from her horn for people as much wealth as the sea, stirred up by the wind, swirls sand. Here the voice is held in suspense (suspensio vocis). The fables say that the river Achelous, which flows in Greece, turned into a bull and fought with Hercules. Hercules struck the horn off the bull and gave it to Abundance, who is Fortune's handmaid, so that she could hand out her mistress's goods with it.
or as many stars as shine in the sky, brought out on star-filled nights,
Or as many stars as shine in the sky at night, when it is starry. And the same goes here.
and did not draw back her hand. Nor drew her hand back to herself.
That is, she did not grow tired of it. And here as well.
the human race would not stop because of that
weeping its wretched complaints. Even so, people would never stop their wretched lamenting. Here the voice is lowered (depositio).
Even if God should willingly receive their prayers,
lavish with much gold,
and adorn the greedy with splendid honours,
what they have gained already seems like nothing. Even if God himself

gladly heard their prayers, was generous to them with his gold, and also gave them the honours they wanted in great abundance, what they had would still not seem enough to them. But savage greed, devouring what it has sought,
opens other gaping jaws.

Rather, great greed, having swallowed one thing, immediately gapes for another. What reins could now hold headlong desire within a fixed limit? Who can hold back greed that is always waiting for more? When it is flowing with lavish gifts, the thirst for having burns all the more. As long as it has enough, it still wants to have more. He who, fearful and groaning, believes himself needy is never rich. He who worries, sighs, and considers himself poor will never become rich. Here the argument (status) ends, because she [Fortune] has defended herself in speech against him as if against an opponent. Therefore Philosophy now speaks to him in her own person.
IN HER OWN PERSON. So if Fortune were to speak to you in her own defence with these words,

"…you would certainly have nothing to mutter against it." If Fortune chose to defend herself in this way, you could not utter a sound against it. "Or if there is anything by which you can rightly defend your complaint, you must bring it forward." Or if you can show that your complaint is just, then you should put it forward. "We will give you room to speak." I give you the chance to speak. "Then I said: These things are indeed fair-seeming, and smeared with the honey of the sweetness of rhetoric and music." Then I said: all these are fair words, as if coated with honey by rhetoric and by music. Since the "sweetness of rhetoric" is mentioned here now for the second time, and no one can understand its sweetness before understanding rhetoric itself, it should not be passed over here. We will say as much as can be said briefly about
what it is.

WHAT RHETORIC IS. Rhetoric is one of the seven liberal arts, that is, the seven book-arts, which few people have learned but many can name. Of these seven, grammar is the first. It teaches us rectiloquium, that is, to speak correctly, which even children can learn, as we hear every day. The second is rhetoric, which leads us further, because it gives us the eloquence that is needed in court and in council, and wherever there is any assembly about common needs. Children are of no use for that, only wise people. Council and court cannot happen without dispute. Where else is there at once such a contest of words as in court and in council? So nowhere is an eloquent man more needed than there. Whoever can settle a dispute by speech, and has learned this in rhetoric, is an orator. In his mouth one finds the sweetness of rhetoric. But if he is unlearned and still eloquent, he can carry out the office of an orator, but he cannot himself be an orator, because what comes from nature does not come from art. Who that knows this sweetness would not gladly hurry to where he can hear it? When in Greece the two most learned men of this art, Aeschines and Demosthenes, agreed on a day to dispute a case in court, did not many thousands come there from all over Greece, as Cicero says? Why, then, should we in particular be unacquainted with so delightful an art? Know, then, that this same science called rhetoric is threefold, because its subject matter is threefold.

ON THE SUBJECT MATTER OF THE ART OF RHETORIC. What is its subject matter but dispute? When a dispute arises, rhetoric has work. Without dispute it has nothing to do, just as medicine is idle when there are no diseases or wounds. If people dispute about right and wrong, as they do in court, that kind of dispute is called in Latin iudicialis (judicial), from iudicium (judgment). If people dispute about appointment to office, such as who is fit to be king or bishop, that kind of dispute is called demonstrativa (demonstrative), because the person's virtue has to be demonstrated. If people dispute about what is useful to do or to leave undone, as they disputed at Rome whether Carthage should be destroyed,

…or would not be. Because one must hold deliberationem about it, that is, resolution and common counsel, that kind of dispute is called deliberativa. After this we should know that each of the three kinds has two subdivisions. Of these two we call the one status legalis and the other status rationalis. When people dispute about the law (legem), and one wants to understand it in one way and another in another way, that status, that is, that dispute, is rightly called legalis. But when people dispute about how reasonable something is that one does or advises, then from the reason, that is, from the ratio, the dispute is called rationalis. It should also be known that people dispute about the law in five ways and about the reason in four ways. It should not weary us to hear about these ways.
WHAT ARE THE LEGAL ISSUES. One dispute about the law is the one called scriptum et voluntas (the letter and the intent). It goes like this.
The rule of the monks says: "After compline let no one speak." When a fire breaks out at night, he cries out to the others
who first becomes aware of it. When he is accused because of the letter of the law, he defends himself by the intent of the writer.
He says that the writer wanted a distinction to be made in this matter. Another kind arises from contrary laws.
These laws, for example, are contrary: "Give to everyone who asks of you," and this one: "Ne aliquid cui nihil" (not anything to him to whom nothing [?]). The third kind arises from ambiguous laws.
An example is in Roman law: "If a harlot possesses a golden crown, let it be confiscated (publicetur)." Which should be confiscated, the crown or the harlot?
The fourth is called in Latin definitio, that is, exact marking-out or exact measuring, because the law uses a word
that can be uncertain and in dispute until its meaning is exactly defined.
For example, it was disputed at Rome whether a man had been justly slain who was killed because
he went about at night with his staff, because Roman law says: "Let anyone caught at night with a weapon (telum) be killed."
Then a definition had to be made of what a telum is. Telum is derived from the Greek word telon, which in Latin means longum (long).
The fifth is called in Latin ratiocinatio, that is, the establishing of one thing from another. An example is how he argued who flogged the exile
that he was entitled to do so for this reason, because Roman law says: "It is permitted to kill an exile caught within the borders."

WHAT ARE THE RATIONAL ISSUES. Of the four rational issues, the first is called coniectura, that is, conjecture, because when the accused denies the charge, people then reach a conclusion by conjecture from signs and arguments. King Solomon did this: "Bring a sword," he said, "and divide the living child in two." The second is called finis, because when the name of the crime is uncertain, it must be defined (finitum). This happens, for example, when sacred vessels are taken outside a church and it is in doubt whether this should be called theft (furtum) or sacrilege. Judges cannot give judgment until the name of the crime has been defined. The third is called translatio, that is, change and misplacement. Change of what? Of place, time, person, charge, or penalty. They argue that it should not take place.

…where it should be, nor when it should be, nor before what it should be. They also dispute that it is not the business of those before whom the accused has been summoned by letter, as often happened at Rome, where people were summoned wrongly. It also happens that someone punishes an offence more severely or more lightly than is right. This dispute is called "exchange" (translatio), because it arises from an exchange. So Gregory accused John of Constantinople of wearing the pallium when he should not, and in the street, where he should not. And Paul accused the faithful of bringing their lawsuits before unbelievers. And so we often say: why does someone take only the money from a man who should have been taken himself, or why does someone kill a man who has deserved a lesser penalty? The fourth rational status is called qualitas.

It takes its name from the fact that it investigates the quality of the deed, I mean whether it is good or bad, right or wrong. But because qualitas has two parts, it must be examined in those parts. What are its parts? They are negotiale and iuridiciale. Negotiale is the dispute that arises over custom, as when merchants argue that a purchase made at the annual fair must stand, whether it is right or wrong, because that is their custom. Iuridiciale takes its name from the same source as the iuridici. At Rome the iuridici were the men who declared the city law in court, and so the dispute named from that word is called iuridicialis. Its parts are also two: absolutum and assumptivum. Absolutum means "bare", because it contains no defence except that the accused says plainly that he was fully entitled to do what he is charged with. So Cicero reports that the poet Pacuvius complained of the insult that a player dared to call him by name there at his house. The player had no other defence than that he was entitled to name him as he was called. Assumptivum is named from the assumptio defensionis, that is, the putting forward of a defence. This status has four parts. One is called relatio, that is, turning back, as Samson turned his guilt back on the Philistines when they accused him and asked why he had burned their crops.

The second part is called remotio, that is, "removal": as the woman, removing the guilt from herself, laid it upon another when she said, "The serpent deceived me." The third part is called comparatio: as that man excused himself by comparison who, to free the army, gave the enemy arma and impedimenta, that is, weapons and provisions, and said that this was better than losing the army itself. The fourth part is called concessio, that is, admission. This issue divides into deprecatio and purgatio, that is, into plea for mercy and excuse. Deprecatio is when the guilty man says, "I have sinned; forgive me," and he does not dispute, but the others who sit in the court dispute whether he ought to be forgiven or not. Purgatio is threefold. One purgatio is called casus, that is, chance. A man excuses himself by casus who says that he was hindered by another man's death, or his own sickness, or some unexpected event. The second purgatio is called necessitas, that is, necessity: as when he has it as his plea that he was captured, or overpowered by force, or thrown into chains. The third purgatio is called imprudentia, that is, ignorance: as Paul excused himself when he said, "I did not know that he was the high priest." These are the examples of the status that arise in court, that is, those that arise in the judicial kind of cause. But those that arise in the demonstrative and in the deliberative kind of cause, where people make speeches, have the same names, but not examples of this sort. From these one can easily recognize those.

WHAT STATUS IS. Next, it should be known that status and constitutio are one and the same, and they are named from the fact that the disputants take their stand against one another. Intentio and depulsio make up the status. The beginning of the dispute is called intentio and depulsio, that is, charge and defense. This is when the accuser says in court to his opponent, "You did it," and he answers, "I did not do it." Or if he says, "You did not do it rightfully," and he answers, "I did it rightfully." When the depulsio is such that it says, "I did it rightfully; I harmed him deservedly," then it must at once have its ratio, that is, its reason, such as: "For he harmed me first." The accuser makes an infirmatio of this ratio, that is, a weakening of it, such as: "For it was not proper for you to avenge your own injury." But if the accused says, "I did not do it; I did not harm him," then no ratio follows such a depulsio, for what reason can a man give who admits nothing? So the accuser must turn to conjectures in order to convict him of his denial. From these two the dispute passes to the others who sit there in court, so that they too begin to dispute whether he did it, or, if he did it, whether he did it rightfully. The judges bring this dispute to an end, for it rests on their judgment whether he is to be held guilty.

or as innocent. And by their judgment he is either acquitted or punished. Before that happens, the orator has to show the mastery of his speech and to bring forward everything by which the case can succeed, and by which whatever he wants to have held right or wrong can be made credible to the judges, and whomever he wants to have held guilty or innocent. Cicero's books on the art of rhetoric are full of how he should proceed in the exordium, then in the narration, then in the confirmation, and finally in the conclusion; and, in all of these, how seemly, how subtle, how playful where that is fitting, how angry,
how threatening, and how varied in every tone of voice he should be. The books that Cicero wrote on the art of rhetoric are full of this.

ON THE PRESENT ISSUE. Now let us also look in this dispute between Boethius and Fortune to see what the charge is and what the rebuttal is. The charge is that Boethius complains like this: "Was Fortune then ashamed of nothing?" And again: "We men are tossed about by the sea of fortune." The rebuttal is that she says: "O man, which of your goods have we taken away? We have done you no violence." The reason for the rebuttal is this: "Riches, honors, and the rest of such things are under my authority.

The handmaids know their mistress. They come with me; when I go away, they depart." This reason is so strong that Philosophy says he cannot immediately make any answer to it. As she says there: "If Fortune spoke to you like this in her own defense, you would certainly have nothing to mutter in reply." With these words she has denied him any means of weakening the reason. And because Fortune is in the right and cannot give up her position, Philosophy wants to instruct him rhetorically. She wants to teach him that he should not long for Fortune's good, since it is so impermanent. Instead, he should desire only the good that, once it has come to him, can never slip away again.
IT FOLLOWS. "They delight only while they are being heard." Such fine speeches

are pleasant only while one is hearing them. "But the wretched have a deeper sense of their ills." But the afflicted carry a heavier load. They feel more of their sorrow. "Therefore, when these things stop sounding in the ears, the deep-rooted grief weighs down the mind." As soon as they no longer hear this, the sorrow that has struck their heart weighs on them again. "And she said: So it is." That is so, she said. "For these are not yet the remedies for your disease." These are not yet the proper medicines for your sickness. "They are only soothing applications for a pain that still resists cure." They are only compresses for your pain, which does not want to heal. "For when the right time comes, I will apply things that penetrate deep." When it is time, I will give you the potions that go right through you. "Nevertheless, do not wish to be thought wretched."
That is, do not consider yourself wretched. But in the meantime, take good comfort and do not count yourself wretched.

ON THE GOOD THINGS RECEIVED. Or have you forgotten the number and measure of your happiness? Have you forgotten your good fortunes, what kind they were and how many? I pass over the fact that when you were left without a parent, the care of the highest men took you in. I will say nothing of how, when you became an orphan, the noblest men took you into their care. And chosen for kinship with the leading men of the city, you began to be dear before you were related, which is the most precious kind of kinship. And chosen for kinship with the noblest men at Rome, that is, chosen as son-in-law to your father-in-law Symmachus, you were dear to him before you became his kin.

That is the foremost kind of kinship, if a man hastens to be dear [first]. Who did not proclaim you most happy, with so splendid a father-in-law, with so modest a wife, and also with the good fortune of male offspring? Who did not call you blessed then, for such a father-in-law and such a mother-in-law, so chaste a wife, and such honourable sons? I pass over the honours you received in youth that were denied to old men. I do not want to speak of how you as a young man won the high office that old men could not win: you became consul as a young man. For it pleases me to pass over what is common; it delights me to come to the singular summit of your happiness. What also happened to others I will pass over. I will come to your mighty and singular good fortunes; of these I will speak.

If any enjoyment of mortal things carries any weight of blessedness, can the memory of that light, that is, of that prosperity, be wiped out by any mass of evils, however great, that rushes upon you? If human prosperity leads to any blessedness, can that brilliant honour then be made void by any misfortune that has happened? When you saw your two sons conveyed together from your house amid a throng of senators and amid the eagerness of the common people. I mean, when you saw your two sons led together from your house with the whole multitude of the lords and with the joy of all the people, so that they brought them with those honours into the senate house and both together received the consulship. When, as they sat in the curule chairs in the senate house, you, as orator of the king's praise, earned glory for your talent and eloquence.

When, as they sat in the senate house on the chair of state, you, as orator, were glorified for your wit and your eloquence in praising the king? It was the custom at Rome, when kings came back victorious from war, that the most eloquent man of all was entrusted with delivering the victory speech in the Capitol before all the people, as was then done for him [Boethius]. But when he says "as they sat in the curule chairs," he says it for this reason: kings sat on the tribunal, where they held court or where they made laws for the people, but magistrates sat in curule chairs when they made city law for the people. They were called "curules" as if "currules," because formerly the consuls, riding to the senate house in a chariot (currus), sat upon it. When in the circus, sitting between the two consuls,

you satisfied the expectation of the multitude crowding around with a triumphal distribution of gifts. Then it was also seen that you, sitting in the middle between the two consuls, generously handed out the victory gifts to the whole multitude.

ON THE TROPHY AND THE TRIUMPH. There were two kinds of victory-honour, the lesser and the greater. The lesser was called in Greek tropheum. That was when the enemies were turned to flight. Then the victor came riding from battle on a white horse. On it he was received by the common people, without the senators. They led him, riding, to the Capitol, and sheep were slaughtered there as a sacrifice. From this the sacrifice was called ovatio. But the greater victory-honour, of which he now speaks,

was called in Greek triumphus. That was when the enemies were slain. Then the victor came from battle riding in a chariot drawn by four white horses. On it the senators, together with the common people, received him and led him to the Capitol, and they sacrificed bulls there. For the common joy, public treasure was taken out of the treasury and given to all the townspeople. The victors were given palms in their hands and a laurel crown on their heads, and the victory was glorified with praise, as was said before. The man entrusted with giving the praise or handing out the treasure was very highly honoured. The word 'sigo' (victory) takes its name from the signa (standards). When the standards are taken from the enemy, that is called 'taking victory'.

ON THE INDULGENCE OF FORTUNE. "You have, I think, deceived Fortune, while she caresses you, while she cherishes you as her darling." I think you deceived Fortune, so that she pampers you so much and cherishes you so much. Demulcet means 'strokes', as one does to someone one fondles. Deliciae are cherished things that we keep for pleasure, not for need, such as turtledoves and parrots. "You have carried off a gift that she had never lent to any private person." You have won from her what she has never yet given to anyone individually, to none of your peers. When she says priuato, she makes an exception only for the king. All who are not kings are called priuati. "Do you then wish to settle accounts with Fortune?" Do you now want to reckon up with her? "Has she now for the first time grazed you with an envious eye?" Only now, looking at you darkly, has she pressed hard on you. "If you consider the number and measure of joyful and sad things,"
"you still could not deny that you are fortunate." If you count up and weigh what you still have of both, sorrow and joy, then you will not yet give up hope of happiness.
"But if you do not consider yourself fortunate for this reason,

because the things that then seemed joyful have gone away, there is no reason for you to think yourself wretched, since the things that are now believed to be sad are passing away." Do you consider yourself unhappy because what gladdened you is gone?

This too will pass away, the thing that grieves you now. So you should not consider yourself wretched. This is called argumentum a contrariis [argument from contraries]. Or have you come only now, for the first time, as a sudden guest onto this stage of life? Have you come here so newly, a guest, onto the stage of this our life? On the stage, by turns, both stories of happy things are performed, such as comedies are, and stories of sad things, such as tragedies are. Because happy and sad things also happen to us by turns, our life is like the stage. Do you think there is any constancy in human affairs? Do you suppose there is any steadfastness in the affairs of men? When a swift hour often destroys man himself? When a short while often destroys even man himself?

For even if chance things rarely keep faith and remain, still the last day of life is a kind of death even for fortune that does remain. Even if there is seldom any constancy in anyone's fortunes, his end is always the end of those same fortunes, even if they had stayed fully with him until then.

What difference, then, do you think it makes whether you leave her by dying or she leaves you by fleeing? What difference do you see in this: whether you leave her by dying, or she leaves you by fleeing from you?
ALL WORLDLY THINGS ARE UNSTABLE. When Phoebus in his rosy four-horse chariot has begun to scatter light across the sky,
the star, dimmed, grows pale,
its white face overwhelmed by the pressing flames. When the morning-red sun, riding on its chariot, as the stories say, begins to shine, the stars grow dark, their pale faces covered by its rays.
When the grove has turned red under the breath of the warm Zephyr,
that is, the rose garden with spring roses,
let the cloudy south wind blow wildly,
and at once the beauty departs from the thorns.
When in spring, from the warmth of the west wind, roses spring up across the field, and then the cloudy south wind comes hot, the flowers must fall from the thorns. In calm, clear weather
the sea often gleams with unmoving waves;
often the north wind stirs up raging storms
and churns up the sea. At one time the sea is still and clear; at another it is churned and turns murky.
If the world's form rarely stays firm,
if it goes through so many changes,
go on, trust in the perishable fortunes of men,
trust in fleeting goods!
It is fixed and laid down by eternal law
that nothing born stays firm.

If the form of the whole world is unstable, and if it changes so often, then go and rely on transient fortunes and on the unstable goods of men! For it is certain and firmly established that nothing born is constant.
LIKEWISE: THAT HE IS NOT DEPRIVED OF ALL HAPPINESS. Then I said, I answered her: "What you recall is true, O nurse of all virtues. What you say is true, teacher of all virtues.

Nor can I deny the very swift course of my prosperity. Nor can I deny my swift, prosperous course. But this is what burns me more fiercely when I think back on it. That is what pains me when I remember it. That burns me.
For in every adversity of fortune, the unhappiest kind of misfortune is to have been happy. No kind of misfortune is so great.

in all misfortunes, this is the one: that a person remembers having once been happy. She said. Then she answered: But the punishment you suffer for a false opinion, you cannot rightly blame on things. You are paying for your false belief; do not blame that on things. Know that you cannot blame them for it. For if this empty name of chance happiness moves you,
you may count up with me how many great things you have in abundance.

Since the bare name of happiness seems so weighty to you, count with me, and try to defeat me: you still have plenty of many good fortunes. What you call good fortune, even if it is not truly so, you have not yet lost. Therefore, if what you held most precious in the whole reckoning of your fortune is still kept for you by God, unharmed and unviolated,
can you rightly complain, when you still keep all the better things?

If God has still kept for you, whole and undamaged, what you held most precious in all your treasure, by what right do you then complain, when you have it, and even have the best, as if you had nothing? And yet that most precious ornament of the human race, Symmachus, your father-in-law, lives on unharmed. Truly, the honor of all men still lives in health: Symmachus, your father-in-law. And a man you would not be slow to buy at the price of your life. And in him you have what you would gladly buy with your life. A man made entirely of wisdom and virtues. He is all virtue and wisdom.
Free of care about his own (that is, his own injuries), he groans over your injuries.

And having [?] for himself, he laments only for you. Your wife lives, modest in character, outstanding in chastity and modesty. Your wife lives, well brought up in all her conduct, surpassing others in chastity and honor. And to sum up all her dowry briefly: she is like her father. And to take in all her dowry together: she is like her father. The goods that a woman brings with her to her husband are her dowry. She lives, I say. She lives, I say. And weary of this life, she keeps her breath only for you. And weary of this life, she keeps her breath in her only for your sake, so that she may see how things go with you.

And she wastes away with longing for you, in tears and grief. In this one thing alone I would grant that your happiness is lessened. And longing for you, she wastes away in weeping and lamenting. In that one thing I am willing to admit to you a lack of happiness. What shall I say of your consular sons? Why should I need to speak of your sons, who were consuls? Consulars are those who were consuls, or who are worthy to become consuls. In whom already
that is, in whom there already shines a sign of their father's or their grandfather's talent, as far as is possible for boys of that age.

In them, indeed, the wisdom of their father and of their grandfather shows itself, certainly as far as it can show itself at that age. Since, then, the chief concern of mortals is to keep their life: O happy are you, if you recognize your own goods, you who even now still have things that no one doubts are dearer than life. Since people hold nothing so dear as life, it is truly well with you, blessed one, if you know what is of value to you: you still have what is dearer than life. In rhetoric, this kind of persuasion is the most honorable and the most powerful: the kind made with the comparative, which can achieve more than the superlative.

Therefore dry your tears. Fortune has not yet come to hate everyone, down to the last one, that is, all without exception. Therefore wipe away your tears. Fortune does not yet hold all of them in hatred. She is still indulgent toward your friends, though she oppresses you. Nor has too violent a storm fallen upon you,

since tenacious anchors still hold, which do not allow you to be without comfort in the present or hope for the future. Nor is too strong a storm meeting you, since the anchor-hooks still hold fast; they do not leave you without comfort, now or from here on. When the wind is moderate, anchors can hold the ship in place; when a powerful storm comes, they cannot. Anchors are heavy, hooked irons, named in Greek after the hand, because they grip fast onto the stones and the ground where one wants to hold the ship in place.

REPLY. "And may they hold fast, I pray," I said. "May they hold," I said. "For as long as they remain, however things may stand, we shall swim out of this. As long as they stay in place, however it may be, we shall come through safely. But you see how much has been taken from our honors. But you see what has slipped away from us of our honors."
AGAIN, PHILOSOPHY ON THE HUMAN CONDITION. But she said: "We have made some progress.

So it is already somewhat better with you now," she said, "if you are not yet weary of your whole lot. If you are not equally displeased with all of what has fallen to you by lot, if you still put your trust in your friends. But I cannot bear your delicacy, you who complain so mournfully and anxiously that something is lacking to your happiness. But it weighs on me that you are so pampered that you complain so wretchedly and so anxiously that anything of your happiness is missing.
For who has happiness so well arranged that he does not quarrel, in some respect, with the nature of his condition? Who is so fully happy

that he does not struggle somewhere over his affairs, over the way they stand? For the condition of human goods is an anxious thing. The nature of human good always leads toward anxieties. And it either never arrives complete or never lasts forever. And it is such that it never comes in full, or if it does come, it still does not last. A man never gets all his affairs in order, or if he does get them in order, it does not last.

DISTINCTION OF THE HUMAN CONDITION. One man has wealth in abundance, but his low-born blood is a shame to him. Some man is rich but is of low birth. Another is made well known by his nobility, but, hemmed in by the narrowness of his household means, he would rather be unknown. Some man is well known for his noble birth, but this grieves him because of his poor household means.
Another, who has plenty of both, weeps over his unmarried life.

That is, if perhaps he cannot find a wife worthy of his birth. Some man has enough of both, and yet he complains that he is unmarried. Another is happy in marriage but has no children, and he builds up wealth for an heir who is a stranger. Some man is well married and yet has no heir; he gathers treasure for people who are not his heirs. Another is made glad by children, but weeps in grief at the wrongdoing of his son or daughter. Some man has children enough, and yet complains that they are wicked. Therefore no one is easily content with the condition of his fortune. So there is no one who has made peace with the condition of his life.
For in each person's lot there is something that the one who has not tried it does not know, and the one who has tried it shudders at. Things befall everyone that are unknown to them!

before they try them, and once they have tried them, those things displease them. Add to this that the most fortunate people are also the most easily hurt. Unless everything is ready at their command, they are cast down by the smallest things, because they are not used to any adversity. Add to that that some man who is blessed in every way is so delicate that if everything is not as he wishes, he is at once upset, even by a little thing, because he is so unused to hardship.
So very small are the things that take the height of happiness away from the most fortunate. Such small things deprive even those who are well blessed

so that they do not become fully happy. How many people do you suppose there are who would think themselves next to heaven if they were granted even the smallest part of what remains of your fortune? How many do you think would consider themselves splendidly fortunate if they had even a small part of your happiness? This very place that you call exile
is a homeland to those who live in it.

This same place that you call exile is home to the people of the land. So nothing is wretched unless you think it is. Surely there is no misery unless a person regards it as misery. On the other hand, every lot is happy if the one who bears it does so with a calm mind. On the other hand, whatever lot falls to a man is happy if he bears it with a calm mind. Who is so happy that, once he has given himself up to impatience,

he would not wish to change his state? Who is there who gives way to impatience and does not want to change his condition, however it stands? With how many bitter things is the sweetness of human happiness sprinkled? Is not the sweetness of happiness mixed with much bitterness? Even if this happiness seems pleasant to the one who enjoys it,

it still cannot be held back from leaving whenever it wishes. It is never so sweet to the one who enjoys it that he can keep it, so that it does not depart when it wishes. It is clear, then, how wretched the happiness of mortal things is. Now it is plain how wretched human happiness is. It does not last forever even with those who have a calm mind, and it does not fully delight the anxious. It never becomes lasting even with the calm-minded, and it is not delightful to the troubled and anxious, even if they have it in full.
[?] ... FROM [PRESENT] HAPPINESS, HE ARGUES THAT HAPPINESS DOES NOT LIE IN PRESENT THINGS. Why then, O mortals, do you search outside yourselves for the happiness that has been placed within you?

Why then, you people, do you seek elsewhere the happiness that you have within yourselves? Error and ignorance confound you. You do not know it; you have made a mistake. That leads you astray. I will briefly show you the hinge of the highest happiness. I will show you what the greatest happiness consists in, and on what it turns. Is anything more precious to you than yourself? Is anything dearer to you than you yourself?
Nothing, you will say. No, you say. Therefore, if you are master of yourself, you will possess what you would never wish to lose,

and what fortune could not take away. If you will rule yourself so that you hold fortune in contempt, then you gain what you will never willingly lose, and what fortune cannot take from you either. By this both will be remedied for you, both the anxiety and the instability of which I spoke before.
And so that you may recognize that happiness cannot consist in these chance things,

reason it out thus. So that you may know that happiness does not lie in these uncertain things, consider it like this. If happiness is the highest good of a nature that lives by reason; if blessedness is the foremost good of human beings. Suspension. And that is not the highest good which can be snatched away in any way. Nor is that the foremost good which one can lose. And here: since that which cannot be taken away is superior. Because only that is foremost which cannot be taken from a person. And here: it is clear

that the instability of fortune cannot attain to happiness. Then there is no doubt that unstable fortune cannot help a person to gain blessedness. The argument says that, because blessedness lies in the highest good, where that is lacking there is no blessedness. That argument is called 'from the cause', because the highest good is the cause of blessedness. To these things: to this I say to you further: the one whom this perishable happiness carries, that is, exalts, either knows that it is changeable or does not know it. For the one whom this fleeting fortune raises up, no other possibility can ever be left [?]: either he knows that it lasts only so short a while, or he does not know it. That is an argument from contraries.
If he does not know it, what blessed lot can there be in the blindness of ignorance? If he does not know it, how can a blessed lot have fallen to him in his ignorance? If he knows it,
he must fear that he will lose what he does not doubt can be lost.

But if he does know it, then he must necessarily fear losing what he knows he can lose. Therefore continual fear does not let him be happy. Therefore the constant fear does not let him be happy. An argument of this kind is called in rhetoric comprehensio, that is, 'capture', because he cannot escape it without being caught. So now it says: whether he knows or does not know that fortune is unstable, he is never happy. So it is in the Gospel: 'Was the baptism of John from heaven, or from men?' Whether they said 'from heaven' or 'from men', they would have been caught. Or, if he loses it, does he think it should be disregarded? Or does he think that, if he loses it, he can console himself for it?

So too it is a very slight good that can be borne with a calm mind once it is lost. So it appears worthless and contemptible, so that it grieves us little when we lose it. All this is dissuasive speech, by which she turns him away so that he does not love fleeting felicity, because that is useless and not necessary.
And since you are the same man who, I know, has been persuaded, and has had it implanted in him by very many demonstrations, that the minds of men are in no way mortal. Suspension.

And since you are the one to whom it has been made known, and into whom it has been impressed by manifold teaching, that the souls of men cannot die. And since it is clear that chance felicity is ended by the death of the body. And here too. And since it is then plain that worldly happiness dies together with the body. It cannot be doubted, if this can bring blessedness, that the whole race of mortals slides into misery at the end that is death. Then there is no doubt, if it gives blessedness, that all men go to wretchedness by dying. This is called an argument from antecedents, because if blessedness dies first,
then misery necessarily follows. But if we know that many have sought the fruit of blessedness not only through death but also through pains and tortures,

how can present happiness make men blessed, when once it has passed it does not make them miserable? If many gained blessedness through death and through other woes, as the martyrs did, how then can present happiness make men blessed, when once it is gone it does not make them wretched? This is called an argument from contraries, since these are contraries: present and passed. They are contraries because one tends away and the other tends hither.
HOW TRANQUILLITY IS TO BE KEPT.
Whoever, being cautious, wishes to set up a lasting seat. Whoever, for safety's sake, wishes to make his dwelling everlasting,
and stable,
and not to be laid low by the blasts of the roaring east wind. He who does not want to be thrown down by the roaring winds. And who takes care to scorn the sea
threatening with its waves. And who does not want to fear the threateningly surging sea:
let him avoid the summit of the high mountain,
let him avoid the thirsty sands. Let him build neither on the height of the mountain nor on the gravel of the shore.
The wanton south wind presses upon the one
with all its strength;
the others, being loose,
refuse to bear the hanging weight. There the wind seeks him out with all its might; here there is no firmness underneath that can bear the building.
Fleeing the perilous lot
of a pleasant seat,
remember to build your house securely on a low rock. If you wish to flee a perilous place by building beautifully, then seek a low stone, on which you may build with confidence.
Although the wind thunders,
mixing the seas with ruin. Even though the roaring wind churns the sea and fells the forest,
you, happy, set within the strength of a quiet rampart,
will lead your life serene,
laughing at the angers of the sky. You will always lead your life in rest, happily lying hidden as if in a fortress, laughing at the weather's unruliness.

HERE BEGINS THE DISPUTATION ON THE THINGS THEMSELVES. But since the soothing remedies of my arguments are now sinking into you, I think somewhat stronger ones, that is, remedies, must be used. Since my words, with which I have tended you until now, are now entering into you, I think stronger arguments must now be taken up. Until now she has spoken with him by persuading and dissuading

according to the art of rhetoric. That is the office of the orator: to urge what is honourable, useful, necessary and possible, and on the other hand to dissuade from what is shameful, useless, unnecessary and impossible. Now she wishes to dispute. That does not concern the orator at all, but the philosopher. To dispute means to treat of the natures of things, or of God, or of morals. Yet we shall see that from here on she begins to do both, both to dispute and to persuade. Come then. Well now, tell me what I ask.
If the gifts of Fortune were not fleeting and momentary,

what is there in them, that is, in the gifts, that could ever become yours, or that would not become worthless once it was examined and considered? If the slippery and fleeting gifts of Fortune were not so, what of those gifts could ever become yours if she did not grant them to you? Or what would you care for those same gifts once you examined them closely? A man has no power to be rich unless Fortune grants it to him, and that same wealth is contemptible in its own nature.
ON MONEY. Are riches precious through your nature or through their own?

Is wealth precious of itself, or because of you? Which of these is it rather? Indeed, which of the two is more precious? Gold, or a gathered heap of money? Do you think gold and the gathered abundance of treasure are more precious than human beings? And yet these shine better when poured out than when heaped up. Truly, they gleam better if one gives them out than if one gathers them. For avarice always makes people hated, and generosity makes them famous. That is plain from this: greed makes people loathed, and generosity makes them renowned and worth speaking of.
But if what is passed on to another cannot remain with anyone,
then money is precious when it is passed on to others through the practice of giving and so ceases to be possessed.

If a man cannot keep for himself what he gives to another, then money should be given for this reason: treasure becomes precious when it passes away through spending. But if all the money there is among the nations everywhere were heaped up with one man, it would leave everyone else without any. Your treasure is like this: if one man takes hold of all of it that there is in the world, the others go without.
And indeed a voice fills the hearing of many people equally and as a whole.

Now the voice is a treasure of this kind: all of it is in everyone's ears at the same moment. But your riches cannot pass to many people unless they are broken up. Your wealth, however, is not shared in any other way unless it is divided up. And when that is done, it must make poor those whom it leaves. When it is divided, those who divide it and let it go are made poorer by that much. O narrow and needy riches, which many cannot have whole, and which come to no one without others becoming poor! Truly, how scanty and how poor is the wealth that many cannot have, and that falls to no one unless someone else grows poorer.

ON GEMS. Or does the glitter of gems draw (that is, entice and delight) the eyes? Do you like to look at gems? Are your eyes fond of their gleam? But if there is anything special in this splendour, that light belongs to the gems, not to people. If there is any precious brilliance in them, it belongs to them and not to human beings. And I am greatly amazed that people admire them. It is a wonder to me that anyone wonders at them.
For what thing that lacks the movement of a soul and the joining together (namely, of limbs) could rightly seem beautiful to a living, rational nature?

What lifeless and limbless thing should seem beautiful to a being with a soul, as man is, and with reason? What should seem beautiful to him is what is like him. Even if these things draw some of the lowest kind of beauty from the work of their creator and from their own distinctiveness, they are placed beneath your excellence and in no way deserved your admiration. Even if, by God's will and by their own colouring, they have something of the lowest beauty, they are still far removed from your high rank, and so they ought not to seem wonderful to you.
ON THE BEAUTY OF THE WORLD.
Or does the beauty of the fields delight you?

Does the field seem beautiful to you? Why not? Why should it not? For it is a beautiful portion of a most beautiful work. It is a beautiful part of the beautiful world. In the same way we sometimes rejoice at the face of a calm sea. In the same way the sea is lovely to look at when it is still. In the same way we marvel at the sky, the stars, the moon and the sun. In the same way we regard the sky itself and all the stars as a wonder. Surely none of these things touches you? Really? Does any of them touch you? Does it give you any of its beauty?
Surely you do not dare to boast of the splendour of any such thing?
Do you dare to boast at all of their beauty? Or are you yourself adorned with spring flowers? Can you be coloured like the flowers? Or does your own fertility swell into summer fruits?

Or are you supposed to become the equal of the summer crops? Why are you carried away by empty joys? Why do you give yourself over to such vain gladness? Why do you embrace outside goods as if they were your own? Why do you prefer other goods to your own? Fortune will never make yours what the nature of things has made foreign to you. Fortune cannot give you what nature has shut you out from.
ON FOOD. The fruits of the earth are, without doubt, owed to the feeding of living creatures.

The fruits of the earth shall, without doubt, be food for the living. But if you wish to supply what nature needs, which is enough, there is no reason for you to seek fortune's abundance. But if you will be satisfied with what nature needs, then you will demand no excess from fortune. For the man who has enough is just as well off as the man who has too much. For nature is content with few things, and very small ones. With few things, and small ones, nature has enough. If you wish to press more on it once it is satisfied, using superfluous things, what you pour in will become either unpleasant or harmful. If you want to add anything more to it, it will be one of two things for you: either unpleasant or harmful.

ON CLOTHING. Now do you think it beautiful to shine in varied garments? Do you want to go about adorned in clothing of many kinds? If their appearance is pleasing to the eye, I will admire either the nature of the material or the skill of the craftsman. If it is pleasing to the eyes, then I praise either the skill of the maker or the material of the work.
ON SERVANTS. Or does a long line of servants make you happy? Does the great number of your servants make you blessed? If they are vicious in character,

they are a ruinous burden to the house, and very hostile to the master himself. If they are of bad character, they are a danger in the house, and a burden, and enemies to the master himself. But if they are honest, how is another's honesty counted among your riches? But if they are virtuous, how then can another man's virtues be your treasure and your wealth?

THAT THE GOODS HE LISTED BELONG TO OTHERS. From all of this it is clearly shown that none of the things you count among your goods is your own good. From all this it is evident that none of the things you take to be your good is your good.
If there is no beauty in them worth desiring, what reason is there for you either to grieve at losing them or to rejoice in keeping them?

And if there is no beauty in them that you ought to desire, what is it, then, that should make you grieve when they are lost, or rejoice when you have them? But if they are beautiful by nature, what does that matter to you? If they are naturally good in themselves, what does their beauty have to do with you? For these things too would have pleased in themselves, apart from your wealth. If they were not yours, they would still be beautiful. Nor are they precious because they came into your riches. Nor does the fact that they are yours make them precious.
But because they seemed precious, you chose to count them among your riches. Rather, you put them away in your own keeping because they seem precious to you.
THAT NEED IS NOT DRIVEN AWAY BY WEALTH. But what do you all want with such a great uproar of fortune? What do you all want to achieve with such a great abundance of your possessions?
You seek, I believe, to drive away need by means of wealth. You want to bring it about, I think, that you lack nothing. But this turns out the opposite for you.
Truly, it turns out quite otherwise. For more help is needed to guard the variety of precious furnishings.

Precious treasure of many kinds also needs a great deal of equipment so that it can be guarded. And that saying is true: those who possess very much need very much. And so the proverb people tell is true: he who has much also needs much. And on the other hand, they need the least – but on the other hand, those need little – who measure their abundance by the needs of nature, not by the excess of ambition: who see to it that they provide their goods according to natural need, not according to the immoderation of greed.

ON ONE'S OWN AND NATURAL GOOD. Is there, then, no good that is your own and implanted in you, so that you seek your goods in external and remote things? Do you then lack, in yourselves, any good of your own, or any that is naturally implanted, so that you seek it in other things? Is the condition of things so overturned that a living being, divine by the merit of reason,
does not seem to itself to shine in any other way than by the possession of lifeless furnishings?

Shall the order of created things now be so overturned that man, who is like God in the dignity of his reason, should not seem beautiful to himself except by possessing a lifeless thing? And other things indeed are content with what is their own: other animals are all content with their own good. But you, who are like God in mind, seek adornments for your excellent nature from the lowest things. But you, who are like God in your mind, want to look for adornment for your excellent nature in the lowest things. Nor do you understand how great an injury you do to your Creator. Nor do you know how great a dishonour you do to God. He wished the human race to surpass all earthly things; you thrust your dignity down below all the lowest things. He wished mankind to be the highest of all earthly things; but you make your lordship lower than the lowest things.

For if everything that is anyone's good (namely, as God is the good of the just) is established to be more precious than the one whose good it is (namely, as it is established that God is more precious than all the just),

then, since you judge the vilest of things to be your goods (namely, not God), you subject yourselves to those very things by your own estimation. If each thing's good is more precious than the thing itself, and you consider the lowest thing to be your good, then you put yourselves beneath it; that is, you are then lower than it, according to your own estimation. This is called an argument from the greater: if riches are greater in value, then the rich are lesser in value. And this indeed happens not undeservedly. That happens to you rightly.
For this is the condition of human nature, that only when it knows itself does it excel other things. The nature of man is so made

that it is above other things only when it knows itself. Yet the same nature is reduced below the beasts if it ceases to know itself. And yet it is lower than the animals if it does not know itself. For in other living creatures it is natural not to know themselves; in men it comes from vice. That is because in animals it is their nature that they do not know themselves, but in men it comes from vices.
THAT NO ONE BECOMES BEAUTIFUL THROUGH OUTWARD ADORNMENT. How widely, indeed, this error of yours extends,
you who think that anything can be adorned with ornaments that belong to something else.

How far your error goes, though, and how many of you are deceived by it, when you think you can be adorned with the outward adornment of someone else! But that cannot be. Now that cannot be. For if anything shines among the things added on, it is the added things themselves that are praised. If something carries anything beautiful on it, people praise what it carries.
But the thing they cover and veil still remains in its own foulness.

But whatever is concealed underneath keeps its ugliness in full. For my part, I deny that anything is good which harms the one who has it. I mean to say that what harms the person who has it is not good. Am I lying about this? Am I lying, then? Not at all, you say. You are not, you say. And yet
riches have very often harmed those who possessed them. Wealth has often harmed the one who had it. For every very wicked man, and the greedier for other people's goods because of it,

thinks himself alone most worthy to have whatever gold and gems there are anywhere. I mean, when some wicked creature, who is so much greedier for other people's goods, thinks himself alone worthy to have all the treasure there is anywhere.
So you, who now anxiously dread the pike and the sword: if you had set out on the path of this life as a traveller with empty hands, you would sing in the robber's face.

So I tell you, you who now worry that someone will kill you: if you travelled through this life bare, you could even sing boldly in front of robbers. O splendid happiness of mortal riches: once you have gained it, you are no longer safe! Well, how precious the blessings of the wealthy are! They are truly so precious that once you win them, you are never safe again. This is called ironic mockery.
THAT THE ANCIENTS WERE CONTENT WITH LITTLE. Too happy was the former age. The earlier world was very happy.
Content with its faithful fields, that is, fertile ones. It was satisfied with what its land produced.
Nor was it ruined by idle luxury, that is, by the excess that makes people idle. It was neither ruined by immoderation nor corrupted by it.
It used to end its late fasts with acorns that were easily gathered. It was in the habit of eating late, and of simple food.
It did not know how to mix the gifts of Bacchus with clear honey. It did not know what [?] was; it had never learned to mix wine with honey.
Nor to mix, that is, to dye, the bright fleeces of the Seres [?, text garbled: 'servm!']

with Tyrian dye. Nor to colour the beautiful silk of the Seres with Tyrian juice. The Seres live far away in the east, next to India. They strip a kind of wool from their trees, which we call silk. It is spun into yarn, the yarn is dyed in various colours, and costly cloaks are made from it. But when people want to make purple, they look in the sea for the creatures that are called conchilia in Latin. These lie enclosed between two shells. The shells bleed when they are broken open, and the purple is dyed with that blood. Because the finest purple is made at Tyre, and that is also where it was first made, he says 'Tyrian'.
The grass gave them healthy sleep. In those days people slept healthily on the grass; they had no feather beds.
The gliding river gave them drink as well. The water gave them their drink.
The very tall pine gave them shade. Trees shaded them; they had no houses.
No stranger yet cut through the deep waters of the sea. Back then nobody yet travelled across the sea.
Nor with chosen goods
had seen new shores. Nor did he land, with merchandise gathered together, on an unknown shore.
Then the savage war-trumpets were silent. Then the perilous war-horns, with which men are now directed to battle, did not sound.
Nor had blood shed in bitter hatreds
stained the rough fields. Nor did blood that came from hostile wounds make the earth bloody.
For why would hostile fury want to be the first to take up any arms? Why should enmity come first? That is, why should anyone be the first to fight out of enmity?
When they saw cruel wounds
and no rewards for blood.

When they saw wounds and no reward for the wounds? Would that our times might now return to the old ways. Would God that these times of ours might turn back to the old customs. But the love of possessing burns fiercely, more savage than the fires of Etna. Now there is nothing of that; instead greed is now kindled, seething more violently than the fire in Etna. Etna burns in Sicily, as Vesuvius does in Campania, and Clemax [?] in Cilicia. Alas, who was he who first dug up the weight of hidden gold, and gems that wished to lie hidden, precious perils? Ah, too grievous! Who was it ever
who first dug gold and gems out of the earth, perilous treasures, which would still gladly lie within if they could?

WHAT THE DIFFERENCE IS BETWEEN RHETORICAL PERSUASION AND PHILOSOPHICAL DISPUTATION. Here you should note what distinction there is between rhetorical persuasion, with which she began at first, and philosophical disputation, in which she is now engaged. When she found him sick in his mind, and he blamed Fortune for it, as if he were pleading against her in court, saying that she had brought him to this, then she had of necessity, since she is a physician, first to heal his mind by clearing Fortune of what he accused her of. She did this with the defenses, so that he should have no expectation of anything better from Fortune.

…and that no one should still expect better treatment from her; and that she cannot become anything other than what she always was; and that if Fortune began to be constant, she would not be Fortune; and that, if she has ever been constant to anyone, it is to him, since he has had her with him longest; and since she has treated him better than others, why does he complain of her? And that she has not yet failed him entirely; and that what may be dearest to him has not been taken from him. And, at the closest point: that she has taken nothing of his own from him, and that she was free to grant him her goods for as long as she wished, and also free to draw her goods back to herself; and that he is sick more from his own impatience than from her injustice. And let him provide himself with whatever advocate he wishes, and she will defend herself well against him in court. Who does not recognize that this speech, and what belongs to it, pertains wholly to the office of the orator? And who does not know that this is the proper play of rhetorical eloquence? What are judges and jurists busy with, if not such disputing? This kind of case is called forensic. Such controversies resound in the forum. In them there is persuasion and dissuasion. With what can one persuade or dissuade in court, if not with the just and the unjust? With what could she now quiet him, except by making him recognize that he has no rightful claim against Fortune? When one begins to show how right or how wrong it is that one person demands something from another, then persuasion and dissuasion succeed. And because she has now overcome his grief

with the satisfactio [?], she therefore now steps down from persuasion to disputation, so that she may thereby fully heal his mind.
