Now let us understand well that in a speech where people sit in deliberation over whether this or that is to be done or left undone, persuasion and dissuasion must be carried out by means of the useful and the useless. As Livy writes, how great a dispute there was at Rome after the Gauls burned the city, over whether they should abandon Rome and move to the city of Veii, which was then wholly in their power, and settle there from then on, or not. Who could have spoken in that dispute about whether it was right or wrong? What had to be argued there was whether it was useful or useless. And all the persuasion

that was used there aimed to make one or the other believable: that it would be useful to do it, or to leave it undone. But in the demonstrative kind of case, when people sit in contentious council over whom this or that should be entrusted to, then in persuasion honorableness is to be cited—I mean that of the man who is being recommended for it—and in dissuasion his baseness is to be cited, if one rejects him. So it went with Cicero when he was made consul out of necessity, because they trusted no one but him to defend them against Catiline and his comrades. Some praised him for his wisdom; others said, as Sallust relates in the Catiline, that the consulship was being defiled because he was born of the equestrian order, not the senatorial. Questions of this kind, since they arise among citizens,

That is why they are called civil (civiles), meaning "of the city" or "of the citizens." As we have said, persuading and dissuading (suasio and dissuasio) belong to these questions. The orator deals with them. The questions that are not civil are philosophical, and they are answered through disputation.

ON THE PARTS OF PHILOSOPHY. Philosophy is divided into the divine and the human. The divine part was taught by those who wrote for us in books about the nature of God himself and the truth of the Trinity. They are called theologians. The foremost of them was John the Evangelist. The human part is taught to us by the physicists and the ethicists, that is, about natures and about morals. The oldest physicist among the Greeks was Pythagoras. After him came Thales and his disciples Anaxagoras and Anaximander

and Anaximenes. They tried to work out what this world was created from. One said it was made from fire, one from water, and one from the divine mind. They also puzzled over these questions: what causes the daily flow and ebb of the sea; what causes eclipses of the sun and moon from time to time; why winter days are short and summer days long; where all the springs of rivers come from; whether the sun or the moon is larger; how large the earth is; what it stands on; and what holds it up. Ambrose later wrote about these and similar things more truly in the Hexameron, and so did others. Bede learned it from them and afterwards wrote it in his book On the Nature of Things. The ethicists are those who teach us to have right morals. The first of these among the Greeks was Socrates, and after him there were many Socratics.

Some of them wrote books on the subject. Among the Greeks, Panaetius did so, and also his son. Among the Latins, Cicero did so in his book On Duties, where he says that he wants to complete what Panaetius left unfinished. They described what human social life (societas humanae vitae), which we call humanity, ought to be like. Cato also took up this subject and wrote in verse in his little book, which begins: "If God is a mind to us, as the poems say." But Terence the comic poet did not teach what morals should be. Instead, he portrayed how corrupt they are among people. That is why he said: "I have described the manners of men, both young and old." That means:

"I have portrayed the manners of people." Later, Ambrose also made sure to write On Duties, that is, what each person's office is to do and what it is his part to do. From it one can learn integrity of life, which makes a person perfect and holy. This disputation leads to the same point: riches cannot make a person blessed, and therefore they are to be despised.

THAT DIGNITIES AND POWERS ARE NOT NATURAL GOODS. "But what should I say about dignities and power?" What can I say about lordship and about power? "By which you make yourselves equal to heaven, ignorant of true dignity and power." These are the things that make you think yourselves as high as heaven, because you do not know the true lordship and the true might. What happiness can they give you?

And what if they fall into the hands of the most wicked man of all? What fires of Etna, belching forth flames, what flood could cause such great destruction? What do they do when they come into the hands of an evil creature? What fire coming out of Etna, or what deluge, does such harm, that is, such slaughter of people? Surely, as I think you remember, your ancestors wished to abolish the consular power, which had been the beginning of liberty, because of the arrogance of the consuls, they who had earlier removed the name of king from the city because of that same arrogance. Indeed, as I think you remember, as you have read, your forefathers wished to do away with the office of the consuls because of their arrogance, although that same office had once been the beginning of liberty. They wished to do this just as they had earlier taken the power of kings away from the city.

Livy tells how Tarquinius Superbus, who was the seventh king at Rome after Romulus, was driven out by Brutus, Collatinus and Tricipitinus and by other citizens who had sworn together against him, because of his arrogance, from which he had his name. He also tells how they agreed to have consuls instead of kings, who were changed every year, so that they would not become arrogant by staying long in power. When in the course of time these too began to practise tyranny, they wanted to destroy that power as well and create new offices that were changed more than once a year, so that those who held them could not fall into any insolence during that time. If power were good in itself, it would not have become so hateful to them. Liberty is of two kinds:

one is the kind that makes a man free, so that he is no one's servant; the other is the one she is now speaking of, which frees him even from royal power, so that he is under no constraint except the common law. But if they are ever given to good men, which is very rare, what else is pleasing in them except the goodness of those who use them? If they also come into the hands of good men, which happens very seldom, what can please in them then except the goodness of those who hold power? So it comes about that honour does not come to virtues from high office, but to high offices from virtue. So you can see that goodness is not adorned by the office, but the office is adorned by goodness.

But what is this power of yours that you so desire and that seems so splendid? What is this power that you pursue so eagerly and that you think so great? Do you not consider, you earthly creatures, who you are and over whom you seem to rule? Do you not know, you creatures of the earth, how lowly you are,
and also those you think you rule over? If you saw among mice one who claimed right and power over the others for himself,

how you would burst out laughing! Well then? If you saw among mice one that grabbed power and might for itself, how laughable would that seem to you? And if you look at the body, what could you find weaker than man? If you consider the body, what will you find more powerless than human beings? They are often killed even by the bite of little flies or by creeping things getting into some hidden part of them. They are often killed just because flies bite them or because something crawls into them.
But how could anyone exercise any right over another, except over the body alone

and over what is lower than the body? Truly, over what can anyone show his power, except over the body, and over what is lower than the body? I mean fortune. I mean his possessions. Will you command anything of a free mind? Can you force anything out of a mind that is its own master by threats? Will you move a mind that holds firm to itself by sound reason from its own state of calm? Do you think you can stir any mind made steadfast by reason from its place and bring it out of its stillness?
When a tyrant thought he would force a certain free man, that is, the philosopher Anaxagoras, by tortures
to betray those who knew of the conspiracy made against him, he bit his tongue, cut it off, and threw it into the face of the raging tyrant. Do you not know this?

When the tyrant thought to force a man who was master of his own mind by torture to reveal to him those who knew of the conspiracy that had been made against him, he bit off his own tongue and spat it at the tyrant, before his eyes. In this way the tortures, which the tyrant thought were material for cruelty, the wise man made into material for virtue. In this way the wise man armed himself for defense with the very thing by which the tyrant meant to show his ferocity.
And what is there that anyone can do to another that he could not himself suffer from another? If a man is powerful, what can he do to another that he cannot suffer in the same way?
We have learned that Busiris was accustomed to kill his guests

and was slaughtered by Hercules, his guest. We have learned that Busiris always slew his guests and sacrificed them to his gods; for that reason his guest Hercules did the same to him. Regulus had thrown many Carthaginians captured in war into chains,
but soon he himself offered his hands to the chains of the victors. Regulus took many Africans captive

and bound them, those whom he captured in war; afterwards he too was captured and bound just as fast. Read Orosius. Do you think, then, that a man has any power when he cannot bring it about that another cannot do to him what he himself can do to another? Do you think he has any power who cannot make sure that the same thing he does to another cannot happen to him? Moreover, if in these very dignities
and powers there were anything of natural and proper good, they would never come to the very worst men.

And besides, if there were anything of natural good in lordships and in power, they would never come to the most wicked. For opposites are not accustomed to be joined together. For contrary things do not stay together. Nature rejects the joining of contraries. Nature does not allow them to mingle [?]. So, since there is no doubt that the worst men very often hold offices,

it is also clear that those things are not good by their nature which allow themselves to cling to the worst men. Thus it is evident, since the most wicked come into offices, that those things which can cling to the worst men are not good. And this can indeed be judged with even more justice of all the gifts of fortune,
which come more abundantly to all the most wicked. This can be said boldly of everything that fortune gives, the greater part of which falls to the worst.
This argument is taken from contraries. On these matters I think we should also consider this: no one doubts that a man is strong when he has seen that strength is present in him.
And it is plain that anyone who has speed is swift.

In the same way music makes musicians, medicine makes physicians, and rhetoric makes rhetoricians. From these things we can also see that a man is known to be strong when strength is recognized in him, and known to be swift when swiftness is recognized in him; and music makes musicians, medicine makes physicians, and rhetoric makes rhetoricians. The nature of each thing does

what is proper to it. The nature of all things does the work that belongs to its kind. These arguments are from cause, because qualities such as strength and speed are causes, that is, the makings and workings of the things that have those qualities, such as the strong and the swift. Nor is it mixed with the effects of contrary things. Nor does it mingle with the contrary workings, as cowardice is contrary to strength and slowness to speed. And of its own accord it drives off whatever is opposed to it. And it readily defends itself against the things that are contrary to it.
Yet riches cannot quench insatiable avarice. Truly, just as strength takes cowardice away from a man,

so riches cannot take away a man's great greed. Nor can power make a man master of himself when vicious lusts hold him bound in chains that cannot be loosed. Nor does power make a man master of himself when his harmful lusts bind him with strong chains. And dignity given to wicked men not only fails to make them worthy, but rather betrays and displays them as unworthy. And dignities, which we call lordship, when they come into the hands of wicked men, do not make them worthy; rather they betray them as unworthy and show them to be so. Why does it turn out this way? Why does it go so? Why can they not do what they promise?
For you delight in calling things by false names, when they are really otherwise.

That is because you want to name things quite differently from what they really are. These names are easily refuted by what the things themselves actually do. Those false names are exposed at once by the working of the things they name. Therefore neither those riches, nor that power, nor this dignity can rightly be called so. Therefore none of them can rightly be called

what they are called: neither what you call wealth, nor what you call power, nor what you call dignity. Finally, the same conclusion may be drawn about the whole of fortune, in which it is plain that there is nothing to be sought and nothing of innate goodness. Finally, I will confirm the same about all worldly fortune: in it there is nothing to be desired, and plainly nothing naturally good. It does not always attach itself to good men, and it does not make good those to whom it has attached itself. It does not always join itself to good men, nor does it make good those it joins itself to.
WHAT DISPUTATION IS. Reasoning carried out in this way belongs to philosophers, not to rhetoricians. One should not argue like this when pleading a case or making a speech.

…but disputations. Such disputation is called disputatio. The name came about because philosophers were in doubt about nearly all questions, as they were on this one: what the highest good (summum bonum) is. Some said wisdom, some virtue, some pleasure. For that reason disputare was first used to mean diverse putare, "to think differently." Now, however, we use disputare for affirming or denying with reasons something that is in doubt. At first the sick man's mind was not in a state for her to dispute with him, since disputation is always subtle and sharp. So she had to lead him, with rhetorical persuasion, which is more delightful and plainer, toward the disputation she is now engaged in.
AN EXAMPLE OF THE PRECEDING STATEMENT.
We know what ruin he caused,
he who once set the city on fire and slaughtered the senators (the fathers),
who killed his brother,

and, savage, grew wet with his mother's spilled blood. We know well what great harm Nero did. He burned Rome and slew the lords of the senate. He slew his brother, and after that he grimly bloodied himself with his mother's life-blood.
And running his eyes over her cold body,
he did not wet his face with tears.

And he did not weep when he looked over her whole dead body. Instead he could be the censor, that is, the judge, of the extinguished beauty, that is, of the body. In other words, he could act as appraiser of his slain mother's limbs. Suetonius says that he often tried to poison his mother because she reproached him for his ways. When he did not succeed, since she had protected herself against it with antidotes, he ordered her to be killed with the sword. He was also curious about all her limbs. So he went over her when she was dead, felt her all over, examined her all over, and then said that some of her limbs were well shaped and some badly.
Yet this man ruled with his sceptre the peoples

whom Phoebus sees as he comes from the farthest east and as he hides his rays beneath the waves. He held power over all the peoples whom the sun shines upon, from its coming in the east to its going down in the west.
those whom the cold northern stars (the Septentriones) bear down upon,
those whom the violent south wind scorches with dry heat,
baking the burning sands again. He ruled over all the northern peoples, and over those to whom the hot south wind brings heat as it parches the sandy land.
Could lofty power at last turn aside the rage of wicked Nero? Could that high power turn Nero away from his wickedness at all?
Alas, grievous fate,
whenever the unjust sword is added to cruel poison! Ah, what a grievous lot has fallen, when the sword becomes the companion [?] of venom. That is to say: when a wicked creature becomes powerful.

THE CONFESSION OF BOETHIUS. Then I said: "You know that ambition for mortal things has had very little, that is, no, dominion over me." "You know well," I said then, "that no worldly desire ever weighed on me. But I wanted material for carrying out affairs, so that my virtue would not grow old in silence. Rather, I always wished for something to do in which my virtue would show, so that it would not grow old unnoticed." "And yet this is the one thing that can entice minds that are excellent by nature, but have not yet been brought by the perfection of the virtues to the final finishing touch."

"Truly," she said, "I know well that this is the one thing that can entice lofty minds. Lofty minds, I say, but not yet brought by the perfection of all virtues to the final polish." That is metonymy: he names the agent in place of its action. It is the custom of workmen, when they complete their work, to polish it at the very end. So too those whose virtues are perfect should polish them with their humility. "Cupido scilicet gloriae" (namely, the desire for glory): their desire for glory is what lures them into public offices. "Et fama optimorum meritorum in rem publicam" (and the fame of the finest services to the state): that is, the reputation of great good deeds, so that these are seen in public life. "Quae quam exilis sit, et vacua totius ponderis, sic considera" (how slight this is, and empty of all weight, consider as follows): how feeble fame is, and how weightless, consider it in this way.

HOW VAIN EARTHLY GLORY IS, SINCE THE EARTH IS NOTHING IN COMPARISON WITH HEAVEN. It is established that the whole circuit of the earth stands in the proportion of a point to the expanse of the heavens, as you have learned from astronomical demonstrations.

"You know well," she said, "that the whole earth, compared with the heavens, stands to it as the measure of a single point, as you learned in astronomy." "Id est, ut nihil prorsus spatii iudicetur habere, si conferatur ad magnitudinem caelestis globi" (that is, so that it would be judged to have no extent at all if compared with the size of the heavenly sphere). I mean that it has no size at all compared with the size of the heavens. Aristotle teaches in the Categories that a point is the beginning of a line and its end, and that the parts of a line are divided by a point, and yet the point, because of its smallness, is no part of the line. What can be smaller than that which has neither length nor breadth? Since it has no part in the line whose end it is, it is likewise no part of the circle whose center it is. In the same way the earth also has no size compared with the heavens, whose center point it is.
Of this region, then, so tiny in the universe,
about a fourth part, as Ptolemy proves and as you have learned, is inhabited by living beings known to us. Of that same earth, so small

compared with the heavens, only the fourth part is settled by people known to us. When she says "known to us", she says it speaking for humankind, because of the Antipodes, since they are unknown to us. We know that water surrounds the earth, and that the fourth part, toward the top, is uncovered; on that the people live. The heavens teach us that it is the fourth part. All who know astronomy recognize that the equinoctial zone divides the heavens exactly in two, and that from it to the outermost poles the distance is the same on either side, I mean to the northern pole and to the southern. The earth is thus round, and we do not know whether it is uncovered on the underside. On the top, where it is uncovered, people live, from the Ethiopian Ocean to the Scythian Ocean.

The people who live farthest to the south live on the Ethiopian islands. For them the sun is directly overhead when it passes out of Aries in springtime, and when it begins to enter Libra in autumn. Those who live closer to us, on the Ethiopian coast, have the sun overhead when it is in Taurus and in Virgo. Those who live closer still, at Meroë, have it overhead when it is in Gemini and in Leo. Those who live closer still, where Syene, a city of Egypt, lies, have it overhead at the solstice, when it enters Cancer. From there human settlement extends northward as far as the island of Thule, which lies farthest out in the Scythian sea. The people who live there live under the northern pole. This is evident from the following:

according to certain cosmographers, there is continuous day there for six months, from the spring equinox to the autumn equinox, and continuous night for the other six months, from the autumn equinox to the spring equinox. This happens because six signs are always hidden from them beneath the earth, so it is night for them while the sun passes through those signs. The other six are always above the earth for them, so it is day for them while the sun passes through those. Since only the six northern signs are visible to them, it follows that the northern pole is overhead for them and is the highest point of all for them. This can be seen clearly on the sphere that was recently made in the monastery of Saint Gall under Abbot Burchard. It shows where all the peoples are located.

And so, when the sphere is set so that the northern pole points straight up, the six northern signs of the zodiac are visible and the six southern ones are hidden. From this we know well that the area from where people begin to live, farthest in the south, to where they live farthest in the north could well be a fourth part of the earth, if seas and marshes did not break it up. If in your mind you subtract from this fourth part all that the seas and marshes cover, and all the space taken up by the vast region, that is, the desert, of thirst, that is, of dryness, scarcely the narrowest area will be left for people to live in. If you then consider how much water, fen and wilderness cut away from this same fourth part, all that is left is a single narrow homestead

for human beings. So in this tiniest point of a point, as it were, enclosed and shut in, do you think of spreading your fame and making your name known? Do you now plan, enclosed and hemmed in within so small a part of so small a part, to spread your reputation and your name far and wide? Or what can glory have that is ample and magnificent when it is squeezed within such narrow and slight limits? Or what can glory have that is powerful and mighty when it is confined by such narrow boundaries? Add this: consider this as well, that this very enclosure, this small dwelling place, is inhabited by many nations that differ in language, in customs and in their whole way of life.

That in this same narrow inhabited region many peoples live who are unlike one another in language, in customs, and in the whole way they live. The fame not only of individual men but not even of cities can reach them, partly because travel is difficult, partly because their languages differ, and partly because trade with them is unusual. Not even the reputation of some cities can come to them, much less that of individual men: partly because travel there is hard, partly because the language is unknown, and partly because trade and every kind of exchange are not customary. In fact, in the time of Marcus Tullius, as he himself indicates in one place, the fame of the Roman republic had not yet crossed the Caucasus mountain. Cicero says that even then, in his own time, Roman power had not become known

beyond the Caucasus mountain. And at that time it was fully grown, and was feared even by the Parthians and the other peoples of those parts. And yet it had grown so great by then that even the Parthians and other peoples there in that plain feared it.

Do you see, then, how narrow and how confined is the glory that you labour to spread and extend? Do you not see now how narrow and how scant the glory is that you want to spread wide and plant far off?

Will the glory of a Roman man go forth where the fame of the Roman name cannot pass? Shall the fame of any Roman man come to a place where Rome itself has no fame? This is an argument from the whole to the part.
What of the fact that the customs and institutions of different peoples disagree with one another?

What do you say to this, that the customs and laws of different peoples disagree with one another? Can that not also lead you astray? So that what is judged worthy of praise among some is judged worthy of punishment among others? So much so that what seems praiseworthy to some seems to others to deserve penalty and retribution. As a result, if anyone delights in having his fame proclaimed, it is of no use to him (that is, it does not fall to him) to spread his name among very many peoples. So it does him no good to spread his name among many peoples, the man who longs for renown. Each man, therefore, will be content with glory spread among his own people. So every man must be content with whatever glory he can have among his own people.
And that very famous immortality of fame will be confined within the borders of a single people. And that very weighty renown, which seems as if eternal, is confined within one country.
But how many men who were most famous in their own times

has the poverty of writers' memory blotted out? How many names that were famous in their own times have been destroyed because writers failed to remember them? And yet what good are the writings themselves, when a longer and dark antiquity buries them along with their authors? And however I discuss it, I cannot see what the writings themselves achieve in this, when old age takes them away entirely together with their writers.

THAT TIME CANNOT BE COMPARED TO ETERNITY. But you think you are extending your immortality when you consider your fame in time to come. You will then gain what seems to you like immortality, when you make yourselves famous forever. But if you weigh this against the infinite spaces of eternity,
what reason do you have to rejoice over how long your name lasts?

If you stretch it out and extend it (I mean the fame spread abroad into future time) to the breadth of eternity, where then is the long duration of your name in which you rejoice? For if the span of a single moment is compared with ten thousand years, however small it is, it still has some share in them, since both spans are limited. If one hour is set against ten years, it has some share in them, even though it is small, because each quantity is measured with certainty and measured exactly.

But this number of years itself, and any multiple of it however large, cannot even be compared with a duration that has no limit. But ten thousand years, and many times as many again, cannot be compared in any way with a length of time that has no end.

For finite things can be compared with one another in some way, but the infinite and the finite never can. Things that have some end can be measured against one another in some way, but they have no measure at all against things that are without end.

So it happens that if fame lasting however long a time is set against inexhaustible eternity, it seems not small but plainly nothing. Hence it is that if long-lasting fame is measured against eternity, it is not small by comparison with it but nothing at all.
But you do not know how to act rightly except for the sake of the breezes of popular favour

and empty rumours. But you do not want to act rightly except for the sake of people's praise and vain fame. And abandoning the excellence of conscience and virtue, you demand rewards from the petty talk of others. And paying no heed to the guidance of conscience, [?] He who claims for himself that he found what another found, and glories in it, acts out of vanity, not out of virtue. You want to be thanked for words that came from others. He who claims what another found and glories in it does not regard his own conscience; he acts out of vanity, not out of virtue. Hear how wittily someone mocked the levity of this kind of arrogance. Hear how merrily one man mocked another who was so boastful and so frivolous.
When a certain man had attacked with insults someone who had taken on the false name of philosopher, not to practise true virtue

but for proud glory, [Raising of the voice] and had added that he would now find out whether the other was a philosopher, namely if he bore the injuries inflicted on him mildly and patiently. And here [?]. The other put on patience for a little while and, having taken the insult, said as if gloating:

"Now at last do you understand that I am a philosopher?" [Lowering of the voice] It once happened like this. A man likewise claimed that he was a philosopher, out of vanity and not out of true virtue. Another man, testing him, greeted him with abuse and said that he would test well whether he really was one, namely by whether he was patient under provocation. Then the first man bore it somewhat patiently, but right afterwards spoke up again, as if mocking him: "Surely now you recognise me as a philosopher?" Then the other said, very bitingly: "I would have understood it if you had kept silent." When the one had said that, the other answered him: "Yes, by God," he said, very bitingly, "I would have recognised it if you had kept silent."
THOSE WHO ARE FAMOUS FOR VIRTUE RIGHTLY DESPISE FAME. But what is it that concerns outstanding men (for these are the subject of the discussion), who seek glory through virtue? What, I say, is it
that fame has to do with them after the body has been dissolved by final death?

But what concerns the most famous men? I mean those who want to put themselves forward by virtue, not by vanity. What concerns them, what use is any reputation to them after death? For if men die entirely, which our reasonings forbid us to believe, there is no glory at all, since the one whose glory it is said to be does not exist at all. If a man dies entirely, in soul and in body, which my reasonings deny, where then is his glory, when he himself does not exist? It is as if she said: where is the accident, when the substance [?] and the accident [?]. But if the mind, well conscious of itself,
once released from its earthly prison, freely seeks heaven, will it not despise every earthly concern, since it enjoys heaven and rejoices that it has been freed from earthly things?

But if the soul, secure, goes to heaven released from the prison of the body, what then is any earthly thing to it, since in heaven it rejoices that it has been set free from earth? What is earthly reputation to it? That is an argument from dissimilarity. Joy and prison are dissimilar, and so are heaven and earth.
THAT FAME IS NOTHING, HOWEVER WIDESPREAD, HOWEVER LONG-LASTING.
Whoever with headlong mind seeks glory alone and believes it the highest good,
let him look at the far-stretching regions of the sky
and the narrow place of the earth.
He who strives eagerly after glory, and to whom it seems the weightiest of things, let him look up at the breadth of heaven and down at the narrowness of the earth.

He will be ashamed of his enlarged name, which cannot fill even that small space. Then he will be ashamed of his famous name, which does not reach even to the end of the narrow earth, and the earth is a single point compared with heaven.
O, why do the proud long in vain to lift their necks from the mortal yoke? What [?] have the proud in mind? Why do they hope in vain to free their necks from the yoke of death?
Although widespread fame, travelling among far-off peoples,
may spread out tongues, that is, of other nations,
and although a great house may shine with famous titles,

death despises lofty glory. Though fame spreads itself, travelling out among distant peoples, and also fills other languages, and though many banners won in battle shine in the house and make the man famous, death never pays any regard to the glory of any of them. It wraps up alike
the humble and the lofty head. It takes the mighty just as it takes the lowly.
And it makes the lowest equal to the highest. And it brings the highest down level with the lowest.
Where now do the bones of faithful Fabricius lie? Where now is the grave of the faithful Fabricius? Who knows?

Where might it be? This is the man who answered the messengers of the Samnites when they offered him their gold and wanted to ransom themselves with it. He said that the Romans did not wish to have gold, but to rule over those who had gold. What of Brutus or stern Cato? Where now is Brutus, or the upright Cato? Brutus won liberty for the Roman people, as was stated earlier. Stern Cato stood with Pompey in defense of liberty against Julius Caesar. And when Julius won the victory, and Pompey, in flight, was slain in Egypt, Cato led the army from Egypt, with Caesar always pursuing, along the whole perilous road that runs from there to the city of Utica. There Cato killed himself so that Caesar would not capture him. From this he is called Uticensis.
A faint fame that survives marks
an empty name with a few letters. The reputation that has barely been left behind marks their name only, with a few letters.
But because we know the splendid names,
is it granted to know those who are consumed? Is it so? Because we know the names, can we from that know the men themselves, who passed away long ago?
You lie, therefore, wholly unknown,
nor does fame make you known. You truly lie in such a way that no one knows you. Nor does fame make you known. No one recognizes you, even though you are still spoken of.
But if you think that life is drawn out longer
by the breath of a mortal name,
when a late day snatches this from you too,
a second death then awaits you.
Do you also think that your life is lengthened by the endurance of your name? What then? When the last day of the world takes that from you too, after that eternal death lies upon you.

LIKEWISE, THAT SHE TURNED HER STYLE FROM DISPUTING TO PERSUADING. Now she turns again from fortuitous things to Fortune herself. All that she says about the things that Fortune bestows, such as wealth, dignities, and powers—how transitory they are, and how they are therefore contemptible—is all disputation. All such reflection pertains to the shaping of morals and the correction of life, in that part of philosophy which, as was also said before, is called ethics. But what Fortune herself is like, as she now intends to tell,

and as she also told before, that is civil, and pertains to rhetorical persuasion, in the kind of case that is called demonstrative. When she defended Fortune against what Boethius had accused her of, that defense was judicial, not demonstrative. Just as there, in the judicial kind, one had to look at equity and iniquity, so here, in the demonstrative kind, one must now look at praise and blame. When a controversy concerns particular persons, it is civil; rhetoric takes it up and settles it by persuading and dissuading. But when it concerns things, it is philosophical, and then one must also settle it philosophically.

Cicero teaches us this distinction, I mean how we should recognize which questions are civil and which are philosophical, with these definitions: "A hypothesis is a controversy set forth in speech that involves definite persons. A thesis, however, is a controversy set forth in speech that does not involve definite persons." Hypothesis means "subpositum" (what is placed under); thesis means "propositum" (what is placed before). When one holds court, when one sits in council, when one sits in an election, that always concerns persons placed under [our eyes], that is, definite persons. But when one deliberates about morals and the conduct of life, or also about the hidden natures of things, that concerns "proposita", that is, things placed far from the eyes. That does not concern the persons who can be placed under the eyes. From this you know

that all that she now wishes to say in praise or in blame of Fortune, because Fortune is a definite person and, as it were, a goddess, she must do rhetorically. By persuading and by disputing one can set a man right about all things. Therefore philosophy is strong in both. Therefore Luke says of Paul in the Acts of the Apostles: "disputing and persuading concerning the kingdom of God." He was disputing when he gave the reason for everything that he taught, and again he was persuading when he said how good, how right, how blessed it would be to do what he taught.

FORTUNE: HOW MUCH BETTER ADVERSE FORTUNE IS THAN PROSPEROUS. "But lest you think that I wage implacable war against Fortune, there is a time when she, the deceitful one, she [deceiving] in nothing, deserves well of men." Do not think, though, that I wish to carry on, as it were, a fixed, implacable war against Fortune.

Deceitful as she is, she is even sometimes good to man; I mean when she is not deceitful. "Namely then, when she reveals herself, when she uncovers her brow and openly declares her ways." She is good then, when she shows herself, when she bares her face and does not hide her nature. "Perhaps you do not yet understand what I am saying." Perhaps you do not yet know what I want to say. "What I am eager to say is a wondrous thing, and for that reason I can hardly unfold the thought in words." What I long to say is wondrous; therefore I cannot say it readily. "For I think that adverse fortune profits men more than prosperous fortune." I truly reckon that misfortune is sometimes better for people than good fortune. "For the former, when she seems flattering,"

"always lies with the appearance of happiness." When prosperous fortune makes herself dear with her charm and seems good to a man, she deceives him with that semblance of happiness. "The latter is always truthful, when she shows herself unstable by her changing." Adverse fortune, however, is truthful when, by changing, she shows how unstable she is. "The former deceives, the latter instructs." That one deceives a man; this one warns him and teaches him. "The former binds the minds of those who enjoy her with the false appearance of goods; the latter sets them free through the knowledge of fragile happiness." That one fetters the minds of those who enjoy her with splendor; this one unfetters them with the sure knowledge of transient good. "And so you may see the former windy, flowing,"
"and always ignorant of herself; the latter sober, girded up, and prudent through the very exercise of adversity."

You can see the one [good fortune] puffed up, unrestrained, not knowing itself; but this one [adverse fortune] moderate, restrained, and made wise by the constant experience of hardships. Finally, happy fortune by its flatteries draws people astray from the true good; adverse fortune often draws them back with a hook to the true goods. That is: in the end the happy one, with her gentleness, causes people to stray from the true good; but the unflattering one sets them back on the way and leads them to the true good, as if pulling them back with hooks.
Or do you think it should be counted among the least of things that this harsh, this horrible fortune has revealed to you the minds of faithful friends?

Do you consider it a small thing that harsh and terrible fortune has shown you your friends in need, who are loyal to you out of true faithfulness? She has separated for you the sure and the doubtful faces of your companions. She has distinguished for you the faces of sure and unsure friends, that is, what kind of people the one group and the other are. In departing, she took away her own and left you yours. In withdrawing, she took with her those who were hers; those who were yours she left to you. How much would you have paid for this when you were untouched and fortunate, as you seemed to yourself? How precious would this not have been to you when you were well off and happy, as it seemed to you?

Stop seeking your lost wealth; you have found friends, which is the most precious kind of riches. Console yourself for your other, lost goods: you have found your friends, who are the most precious treasure.

ON THE DUTY OF THE ORATOR. Here you can learn how one should persuade someone toward a thing that is hateful to us and that we therefore shun, as all people do: adverse fortune. One can entice us toward it if one begins to tell us of so many virtues in it and to promise so many pleasant things, as Philosophy now does concerning this same adverse fortune. She makes it dear to us in two ways: both by praising it and by reproaching prosperous fortune. Who could trust adverse fortune to bring any good? The very name of adversity

makes it hateful. Against that, the name of prosperity makes itself pleasing; it is so called from the following wind, that is, "a porro spirando" (from blowing forward). But since there is now nothing stable in prosperous fortune, as she [Philosophy] charges against it, nor anything certain, and since it entices people and ensnares their minds, and by acting very kindly pretends to be what it is not, and when one expects everything one wishes from it, it then suddenly changes and thrusts that person away — to whom then should it seem good? But if adversity is the teacher of virtue, and leads to God, and makes people perfect and worthy of heaven, as she has praised it, should it not then rightly seem good to us? What can be stronger for persuading than praise? Rhetoric says

that the duty of the orator is to speak appropriately for the purpose of persuading, that is, to speak persuasively. Is this not spoken persuasively? Who can do this as well as Philosophy? Therefore we should believe her that adverse fortune is better than prosperous fortune.

On the love that makes friendships firm and binds all things. That the world, with steadfast faith, varies its harmonious changes. Suspension [suspensio]. That is, the world varies the harmonious courses of the four seasons with firm faithfulness. Summer and winter, spring and autumn differ from one another because none of them is like any other. And yet they are alike, because none of them disturbs another. That the warring seeds keep a perpetual covenant. And here. That is, the four discordant elements, which are the seeds, as it were, of all bodies, keep an eternal concord.

They are opposed to one another, and yet they are together in all bodies. That Phoebus in his golden chariot brings forth the rosy day. And here. That is, the sun, riding on a beautiful chariot, brings the day. That Phoebe should rule the nights that Hesperus has brought on. And here. That is, his sister the moon rules the night that the evening star brings on. That the greedy sea (that is, greedy to break out) keeps its waves within a fixed limit, so that the wandering (that is, waves) may not stretch their broad bounds over the lands. That is, the sea too, which would gladly break out, holds back its restless waves at a fixed boundary, and does not let them (I mean those same waves) go any farther beyond the shores onto the land. This chain of things is bound by love, which rules the lands and the sea

and commands heaven. Resolution [depositio]. Love makes this order of things firm: it rules and constrains the earth and the sea, and it governs in heaven. Which love is that? That is God himself. If it should slacken the reins, whatever now loves mutually would at once wage war. If it lets go of the bridle, whatever is now bound in love at once begins to fight. And the machine that they now drive with beautiful motions in allied faith, they would strive to break apart. And this structure of the world, which they now, of one mind, cause to run its course beautifully, they would hasten to break apart.
It also holds together peoples joined by a sacred covenant. The same love also holds human beings together in holy concord. It also binds the sacred bond of marriage

with chaste loves. It also makes lawful marriage firm with pure loves. It also lays down its laws for faithful companions. Even for companions who truly love one another, it establishes law. O happy race of men, if the love by which heaven is ruled should rule your minds! Truly, you human race, how blessed you are if the love that rules heaven rules your mind! Here ends the second book of Boethius.
Here begins the third book.
She had now finished her song. She ended the song. When the sweetness of the song had held me spellbound, eager to listen and astonished, with my ears still pricked up.

Even then the sweetness of the song made me keep listening; such longing and such wonder did it stir in me. And so a little later I said. After a while I said: O highest comfort of weary minds! Especial comfort of the sorrowful! How much you have refreshed me, both by the weight of your sayings and by the delight of your singing. How much stronger you have made me by the weight of your speech and by the delight of your song. So much that I now think that after this I am not unequal to the blows of fortune. You have done this so fully that from now on I will not believe that I yield at all to the blows of fortune.
I can bear them well. And so the remedies which you said were rather sharp, not only do I not dread them, but, eager to hear, I earnestly demand them.

Therefore I do not fear the stronger remedies of your speech, and I will gladly hear them, and I demand them. Then she said: "I perceived it when, silent and attentive, you were seizing upon our words." "Indeed," she said, "I became aware of that when you were silent, when you listened closely to my words. And I waited for that disposition of your mind, or, what is truer, I myself brought it about." And I waited for this until your mind became such, or, what is truer,
I made it so. For the things that remain are such that, when tasted, they bite, but once received within, they grow sweet.

The things still to come are such that they sting when you taste them, but once swallowed they seem sweet. "But as for your saying that you are eager to hear: how much ardor you would burn with, if you knew where we are undertaking to lead you!" "But as for your saying that you would gladly hear: oh, how earnest you would be about it, how you would burn, if you knew where I have begun to lead you!" "Where then?" I said. "Where then?" said I.
"To true happiness," she said. "To the true happiness!" she said. "Of which your mind too dreams.

Of which you too dream in your mind. But because its sight is occupied with images, it cannot behold that happiness itself. But while it looks at the image, it cannot see the thing itself. As long as you think of worldly happiness, so long are you thinking of the image of true happiness, not of true happiness itself." Then I said: "Do it, I beg you, and show me without delay what that true happiness is." "For God's honor," said I, "do that, and show me the true one without delay." "I will do it," she said, "gladly, for your sake." "Now I will do that," she said, "gladly, for love of you. But the one that is better known to you,

I will first try to describe in words and give it shape, so that, once you have examined it, when you turn your eyes to the opposite side, you may recognize the pattern of true blessedness. But first I will depict for you worldly happiness, which is better known to you, so that afterward, when you have looked through this one, you may look over there and recognize the other all the better, and see what difference there is between them."
SHE IS ABOUT TO GIVE THE REASON WHY SHE DELAYS. Whoever wishes to sow a fertile field
first frees the land of roots. Whoever wishes to sow a good field first clears it of weeds.
With a sickle he cuts back brambles and fern,
so that Ceres may come heavy with new grain. He removes the fern and briars with the clearing-sickle, so that better grain may grow for him on the newly cleared land.
The labor of the bees is all the sweeter
if a bad taste has first consumed the mouth. Honey too is all the sweeter if the mouth has first tasted something bitter.
The stars shine more pleasingly
when the south wind ceases to make its rain-bearing sounds. And the stars shine more brightly when the rain-winds die down.
When the morning star has driven away the darkness,
the beautiful day, that is, the sun, drives, that is, brings forth, her rosy horses. And when the morning star drives the night away, the sun shows her red horses; she comes riding upon them.
You too, looking first upon false goods,
begin to draw your neck back from the yoke.

…true things will then enter the mind. So you too must do: first recognize false happiness and try to free yourself from it. Then the true things will come into your mind. Otherwise you will not succeed.

THAT ALL STRIVE TOWARD HAPPINESS, THOUGH NOT BY THE RIGHT PATH. Then, with her gaze fixed for a little while, and as if she had withdrawn into the august seat of her mind, she began thus. Then, looking a little toward the ground, and as if resting in her mind as on an imperial throne, she began thus.

All the care of mortals, which the labor of many different pursuits keeps busy, goes forward by different paths. The cares of all people have gone different ways, the cares that many kinds of struggle and many kinds of effort drive and stir up in them. Yet it strives to reach one end, that of happiness. Yet they all aim at one place, because they all aim at happiness.
And that is the good which, once someone has obtained it, leaves him able to desire nothing further. And that is the good: if anyone gains it,

then once he has gained it, he can desire nothing further. This is indeed the highest of all goods, and it contains all goods within itself. That is the foremost of all good, holding all good within it. If anything were missing from it, it could not be the highest. If it lacked anything, it would not be full. For something would be left outside it that could still be wished for. For apart from that, there would still be something a person could desire. That is an argument from the part: where one part is missing, the thing is not whole.
DEFINITION. It is clear, therefore, that happiness is a state made perfect by the gathering together of all goods. Therefore it is plain that happiness is the fullness of all good.

If you would rather say 'the full state of all good', that is the same thing. As we said, all mortals try to obtain this by different paths. As I said, all people hurry to gain that happiness. They all hurry toward it, along different ways. For the desire for the true good is planted by nature in human minds. That is because the human mind is turned by nature toward the true good. But error, straying from the way, leads them off to false things. But mistaking the way leads them astray to what is false.
RICHES. Some of these, believing that the highest good is to lack nothing, labor to have riches in abundance. Some of them strive
to become rich, because they consider it best of all to need nothing.

HONORS. Others, judging the good to be whatever is most worthy of reverence, gain honors and strive to be revered by their fellow citizens. Some, thinking that being worthy of honor is the good, hurry to win honors so that they may be held in awe by their fellow citizens.

POWER. There are those who place the highest good in the highest power. Then there are those who think power is the best thing. These people either want to rule themselves or try to attach themselves to those who rule. They want to become powerful themselves, or always to be with the powerful.
FAME. But those to whom fame seems the best thing,
these hurry to spread a glorious name, through the arts either of war or of peace.
Those who like fame best want to make their name glorious through some of the skills that are needed at home or in the army.

PLEASURE. But very many measure the fruit of the good by joy and gladness. Some think the best gain lies in delight and in joy. These think it most blessed to melt away in pleasure. They think it blessed to live with pleasures and to swim in them.

ONE FOR THE SAKE OF ANOTHER. There are also those who swap the ends and the causes of these things with one another. So there are also those who love this for the sake of that, and others who love that for the sake of this, and so have exchanged them.
For example, those who desire riches for the sake of power and pleasures, or those who seek power

either for the sake of money or to spread their name. That is how it goes when some seek wealth for the sake of power and pleasure, and others, on the contrary, seek power for the sake of wealth and fame. What a person uses to go further is the cause; where he wants to get to is the end. One can also say it this way: what he uses to aim at something is the cause, and what he aims at is the end.
WHAT IS ADDED TO THESE. In these things, then, and in others like them, the purpose of human actions and wishes is engaged.

These and similar things are what people's deeds and wills aim at. Such things are nobility and popular favour, which seem to win a certain renown. That is how nobility works, and the praise of the people, which serve to bring fame. Wife and children are sought for the sake of pleasantness. That is how wife and children work: people seek them for delight. But friendship, which is the most sacred kind of thing, is counted not under fortune but under virtue. What about the delight of friends? It is not of that kind. It is holy, so it belongs not to false happiness but to true happiness, which is where virtue belongs.

The rest is taken up either for the sake of power or of delight. Everything I named of another kind is acquired out of love of power and for the sake of pleasure. And now it is plain that the goods of the body are referred back to the higher goods named above. Now it is also clear that the body's advantages lead back to those same five. For strength and size seem to give power: strength and size give might. Beauty and swiftness give renown: beauty and swiftness give fame. Health gives pleasure: health gives joy. From all of these it is clear that happiness alone is desired. All of them are desired for the sake of one thing, happiness.
PROPOSITION. For whatever each person seeks above everything else, he judges to be the highest good. Whatever each person strives for most eagerly, he considers to be the best.
ASSUMPTION. But we have defined the highest good as happiness. And we have said that happiness is the best.
CONCLUSION. Therefore each person judges the state he desires above all others to be happy. So each person considers the state he seeks most eagerly to be blessed.

HOW GREAT THE FORCE OF THE SYLLOGISM IS. A syllogism does not deceive if it is properly made. It is properly made when it has the three parts it should have in dialectic: two of them must be so true that everyone can grant them, and they must hold together so that they prove the third true even without anyone granting it.

Take this example: Jacob was the son of Isaac, and Isaac was the son of Abraham. Those are two premises. If someone grants these, he must necessarily grant the third, that Abraham was Jacob's paternal grandfather. For this reason the logic of the syllogism we meet here is also clear: Whatever each person most desires to obtain, he considers the highest good. Now the highest good is happiness. Those are two premises. Whoever grants these must grant the third, even against his will, which says: Whatever each person most desires to obtain, he considers happiness. From this we should know that an argument consists of one premise or of two.

An argument of one premise goes like this: If Jacob was the son of Abraham's son, then he was Abraham's grandson. That single premise is called the proposition. An argument of two premises goes like this: If Jacob was the son of Abraham's son, then he was his grandson. And he certainly was. That is the proposition and the assumption. But if it says, "Jacob was the son of Abraham's son, and therefore he was his grandson," then that is the proposition and the conclusion. Therefore an argument is an imperfect syllogism. If you complete it to three premises, then it is a full syllogism. "So you have almost" (that is, "almost" because there may be more) "the form of human" (that is, false) "happiness set before your eyes." Now I have shown you, very nearly, the picture of human happiness:
"Wealth, honors, power, glory, pleasures." I mean riches, honor, power, fame, and delight.
"Considering these alone, Epicurus accordingly decided for himself that the highest good is pleasure." Epicurus was one of the philosophers

who joined them in seeking the highest good. He did not know God or spiritual goods, and since he thought only about these five, he accordingly chose to take pleasure as the highest good. "Because all the others seem to bring delight to the mind." He chose it "accordingly" because, as it seemed to him, those four give delight to the mind just as pleasure gives delight to the body. Therefore he thought that those four were included in this one, and that in it alone he had found what he was seeking. "Epicuros" in Greek means "over pigs" in Latin. The other philosophers gave him that name because, by following pleasure, he and his followers lived like pigs.
THAT PEOPLE DO NOT ERR IN THE GOAL BUT IN THE WAY, AND THAT NONE OF THE THINGS WRITTEN ABOVE IS THE HIGHEST GOOD. NONE OF THE ABOVE-WRITTEN [?] "But I return to the pursuits of men,"

FIVE [?] TO BE LACKING. "whose mind seeks its own good again, even though its memory is clouded." "Now I want to tell you again," she said, "what people strive for. Their mind always aims at its good, even if it aims at it without clear memory." "But like someone drunk, it does not know by which path it should return home." And yet, as if it were drunk, it does not know by which road it should turn back home. It seeks what ought to be sought, but it does not go after it rightly.

WEALTH. "Do those people seem to go wrong who strive to lack nothing?" Do you think those people go wrong in their minds who would like to be in need of no good thing? No, they do not. "And yet it is nothing other [than]"

...that could bring happiness to perfection as well as an abundant state of all goods. Truly, nothing can fulfil happiness as well as an abundant state of every good. Not in need of anything from others, but sufficient to itself. It has no need of anything outside itself, and it has enough from itself.
HONOUR. Are those mistaken who think that what is best is also most worthy to be honoured with reverence? Do they err, do you think,

those who consider the best to be the most worthy of honour? Not at all. No, they do not. For a thing is not base and contemptible when almost all mortals strive to obtain it. What all people hasten towards could not be contemptible. They hasten to the highest good, and where they find that, they have also found what is most worthy of reverence.

POWER. Or is power not to be counted among the goods? Should one not consider power good? That is, should one not be certain of having power along with the highest good? What then? How does it seem to you? Is that which is agreed to be more excellent than all things to be thought weak and without strength? That which is foremost of all things, that is, the highest good, how could it be without strength?

FAME. Or is renown to be counted as nothing? Should fame seem of little worth to a man? But can it be set apart? Whatever is most excellent must also seem most renowned. But how could it be otherwise, since what is also foremost is necessarily the most famous?

PLEASURE. For what need is there to say that happiness is not anxious and sad, and not subject to pains and troubles, when even in the smallest matters people seek what is delightful to have and enjoy? What need is there, then, for me to deny that the highest good and happiness, which they strive for, have any discomfort at all, since they seek even trivial things for the sake of pleasure? In the highest good nothing is more fully present than pleasure. And these are the things that people wish to obtain.
Without doubt these are the things people long for. And for this reason they desire riches, high offices, kingdoms, glory, and pleasures,
because they believe that through these they will gain sufficiency, reverence, power, renown, and joy. And for that reason they want wealth,

lordship, power, glory, and pleasure, because they think that with these they will have sufficiency, honour, might, renown, and joy. What would wealth be to them if they did not have sufficiency? What would lordship be to them if it did not give them honour? What would power be to them if it did not make them mighty? What would glory be to them except for the sake of renown? And what would delights be to them if they did not make a person glad? So it is the good that people seek through such different pursuits. It is always one thing, one good,

that people strive for in so many ways. This easily shows how great the force of nature is: though opinions vary and disagree, they still agree in loving the good as their end. From this one can easily see how strong nature is, when such conflicting ways agree on the end they all hasten towards, the good.
ON THE POWER OF NATURE. How many reins of things
mighty nature steers,
by what laws, in her foresight, she preserves the boundless world
and holds it fast,
binding each thing with a bond that cannot be loosed: this it pleases me to set forth in clear-sounding song.
with pliant strings. How mighty nature turns her reins, by what law she preserves this world, and how she binds things with a firm bond, that I will sing aloud on supple strings.
Although Punic lions
wear beautiful chains
and take the food given them by hand

and, used to suffering blows, fear their harsh master. Although the bold lions wear chains on them, and although they are fed from the hand because they are tame, and although they fear their master because they are used to his blows,
if blood has stained their fearsome mouths,
their spirits, long dormant, return,
and with a deep roar they remember themselves. If they taste blood, their former fierceness rises up in them at once, and at once they remember what they are, gnashing their teeth after their kind.
They free their necks from the loosened bonds [?].
And the first tamer, torn (that is, lacerated) by the bloody tooth,
is the first to stain their raging wrath. At that moment they break the chains and attack the master first. He becomes the first victim, and as they tear at him with their teeth, their fury grows.
LIKEWISE. The chattering bird that sings on the high branches
is shut up in the hollow of a cage. And the bird that goes singing from tree to tree is caught and put in a cage.
Although human care may serve it cups smeared with honey
and lavish meals, playing with sweet zeal,
although after that people serve it honeyed things and every abundance, as many do, for pastime and for play,
yet if, hopping out of its narrow shelter,
it sees the pleasant shade of the groves,
it tramples the scattered food with its feet;
sorrowful, it seeks only the woods;

it murmurs of the woods with its sweet voice. If it manages to escape from the cage to the wood, where it sees its beloved shade, then the earlier food means nothing to it. In the forest alone it wants to live; in the forest it wants to twitter.
LIKEWISE. A branch once bent by strong force
bows its top downward. The top of a young tree is also sometimes pulled down by force.
If the right hand that bent it lets it go,
it looks at the sky with its top held straight. If it is released, it straightens itself up again toward heaven.
LIKEWISE. Phoebus sinks into the western waves,
but turns his chariot again by a secret path
to his accustomed rising. The sun also goes westward in the evening to its setting. But in the morning it comes back by a hidden course to its rising.
LIKEWISE. All things seek again their own return,
and each thing rejoices in its return. Everything has its way back, and always strives toward the place it belongs to by nature.
Nor does any set order remain for anything,
unless it has joined its rising to its end
and made its own circle stable.

No other thing remains in its natural order unless its end reaches back to its origin and it makes itself stable in the manner of a ring. Therefore man keeps to his nature if he can find his way back to God, from whom he came.

THAT ERROR DRAWS BACK FROM WHERE NATURE TENDS. Yet you too, O earthly creatures, dream of your origin, though in a faint image. So do you men also: however faint the image may be, you still always see your beginning, as if through a dream. The first transgression has taken this from men, so that although they seek their origin, they cannot clearly recognize it. And you look ahead to that true end of happiness with some kind of thought, though hardly a perceptive one. And you look straight ahead to the blessed end, however much you do so with an undiscerning mind.
And natural inclination leads you there, to the true good, and manifold error leads you away from it.
Therefore, that is: because nature is strong, it leads you straight to the highest good, striving toward it; and because it has been corrupted, error leads you astray.

HE SAYS IT MUST BE PROVED BY ARGUMENTS WHETHER WHAT IS DESIRED CAN BE ATTAINED THROUGH THESE FIVE. For consider whether, through the things by which people think they will attain happiness, they can reach the destined end. Now consider whether, with those five things by which they trust to gain happiness, they can come to where they strive to go. For if either money
or honors and the rest bring something such that nothing good seems to be lacking, we too would admit that some people become happy by obtaining them.

If such things as treasure and honor can help anyone so that he lacks no good, then let us grant happiness to those who gain any of them. But if they cannot accomplish what they promise, and lack many goods, is not a false appearance of happiness clearly found in them? But if they cannot deliver what they promise, and they lack much good, then they are plainly a deceptive image of happiness.

FIRST PROOF, CONCERNING RICHES. First, then, I ask you yourself, who a little while ago abounded in riches. Now first tell me, you who were rich just recently: amid that most abundant wealth, did anxiety arising from some injury never trouble your mind? When you were at your richest, did anything distressing ever happen to you through anyone's fault, so that your mind was troubled?
"And yet," I said, "I cannot remember ever having been free in mind

…without always being troubled about something. "Truly," I said, "as far as I remember, I was never so free in my mind that I did not worry about something." "Was it not because either something was absent that you did not want to be absent, or something was present that you wished were not present?" "Was that not because," she said, "you lacked something dear that you did not want to lack, or had something hateful that you did not want to have?" "It is so," I said. "That is so," said I. "So you desired the presence of the one and the absence of the other." "Then you desired," she said, "the presence of the one
and the absence of the other." "I admit it," I said. "I admit that," said I. "But each person," she said, "lacks what he desires."

"So a man is in need," she said, "of what he desires." "He lacks it," I said. "He is in need," said I. "But whoever lacks something is not entirely sufficient to himself." "Whoever is in need of anything," she said, "is not sufficient in all things." "Not at all," I said. "He is not," said I. This is an argument from the part. As if she said: "Whoever lacks some of the parts does not have the whole."
"So you endured this insufficiency," she said, "while you were full of wealth?"

"Did you suffer this need," she said, "when you were very rich?" "Why not?" I said. "How could it be otherwise?" said I. "Then wealth cannot make a person lack nothing and be sufficient to himself." "If this is so," she said, "then riches can never make anyone free of need or sufficient." "And this was what they seemed to promise." "And yet they pretended to do that."
ALSO. "And I think this too must be considered most carefully: money has nothing in its own nature that prevents it from being taken away from those who own it against their will."

"This too must be carefully considered: treasure has no power in itself that prevents it from being taken against their will from those it belongs to." "I admit it," I said. "I admit that," said I. "Why would you not admit it?" "Why should you not admit it?" she said. "Every day someone stronger snatches it from a person against his will." "Every day whoever is more powerful takes it from someone else against his will. For where do lawsuits in the courts come from?" "Where else do the complaints in court come from,

and the outcries in court? They come only from people reclaiming money that was taken from them against their will, either by force or by fraud." "They come only from treasures taken from the unwilling by force or by treachery
being demanded back."

"It is so," I said. "That is so," said I. "So each person," she said, "will need protection sought from outside to guard his money." "So everyone," she said, "needs another man's help to protect and defend his treasure."

"Who would deny that?" I said. "Who can deny that?" said I. "Yet he would not need it (that is, protection) unless he owned money that he could lose." "He would have no need of that help," she said, "if he did not have the treasure

that he fears to lose." "That cannot be doubted," I said. "There is no doubt about that," said I. "So the matter has turned around into its opposite." "If this is so," she said, "then the thing [?] has been turned the opposite way.
For wealth, which people thought would make them sufficient to themselves, instead makes them need someone else's protection." I mean by this

that the riches that were supposed to make them sufficient on their own make them need other people's help. This is an argument from the outcome. As if she said: "Since [?] it turns out that the rich are in need, riches are the cause of need."
